Existing persuasive dialogue systems are largely single-session, static, and unimodal, while cross-session memory systems, though temporally aware, retain only factual content and overlook persuasion-specific dynamics. We propose MERIT (Memory-augmented Experience-Rationale for Iterative Temporal persuasion), which pairs a graph-based memory of four persuasion-specific memory types with a per-persona experience rationale library that records which strategies succeed for each user and why. Together they enable adaptive persuasion through prompt composition alone, with no parameter updates. To support this setting, we introduce PERSIST (PERSona-driven InSurance Interactions over Time), a dataset of 60 curated personas spanning 10+ years of motor insurance renewal interactions, with probabilistic life events that shift negotiation behavior and receptiveness across sessions, verified through strict human-in-the-loop annotation. MERIT surpasses memory and experience-based baselines on every metric across two policy backbones, reaching persuasive-appeal scores of 4.10 and 4.74 (out of 5).

candidates.title: Ref2Light: From One Image to Interactive Glasses-Free 3D Characters
candidates.abstract: Animating character illustrations on light-field displays demands coherent binocular parallax, real-time pose articulation, and fine-grained expression control. However, existing 2D animation and 3D reconstruction pipelines cannot combine these with rapid character switching. We present Ref2Light, a feed-forward framework that maps a single A-pose illustration and continuous pose and expression controls to display-native light-field animation, without per-character 3D reconstruction, rigging, or test-time optimization. Our key insight is to decompose light-field synthesis into static identity, view-dependent parallax, and control-driven articulation. A shared encoder caches multi-scale identity features once per character for rapid switching. A conditional decoder then synthesizes ordered angular anchors from these features via backward texture transport and direct color synthesis. A global-local control scheme deforms the anchors with head-body controls and uses the updated correspondence fields to track facial regions across views for masked local facial refinement. Finally, calibrated differentiable subpixel interlacing converts the anchors into the native panel raster, enabling end-to-end native supervision without rendering all views at full resolution. On held-out VRoid identities, Ref2Light reduces head-body LPIPS by 20.1%-55.6% over 2D and 3D baselines and lowers non-target change MAE in mouth closure by 95.6%-96.5% versus monolithic decoding, while running at 34.0-40.1 FPS for 1440x2560 native rasters on a consumer GPU. Code and demo are in the Supplementary Material.

candidates.title: CrysLDM: Latent Diffusion Model for Crystal Material Generation
candidates.abstract: Generating new crystal materials with desirable chemical properties has long been a challenging task. Existing diffusion models operate in feature space, requiring complex diffusion architectures to model the joint distribution of atom types, coordinates, and lattice structures. This complexity increases the number of diffusion steps, leading to higher training and sampling costs. In this work, we aim to generate novel crystal materials within a time- and resource-constrained setup, where existing models are not well-suited. To address this, we propose CrysLDM, a novel latent diffusion model for 3D crystal materials, which integrates a variational autoencoder and a diffusion model. The VAE encoder maps 3D crystal structures into a latent space, where the diffusion model operates. Since CrysLDM leverages a smooth, lower-dimensional latent space, it simplifies the generative process and accelerates both training and inference. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets and tasks, we show that CrysLDM generates stable and valid materials with quality comparable to state-of-the-art methods, while being significantly more efficient in terms of computational resources and time.

candidates.title: DeclareViT: Decoupling Early Classification from Feature Refinement with Exit Query for Efficient ViTs
candidates.abstract: Vision Transformers achieve remarkable recognition performance but incur substantial computational cost during inference, limiting their use in latency- and compute-constrained deployment scenarios. Early-exit inference offers a promising solution by allowing easy samples to terminate at intermediate layers. However, existing approaches typically couple early classification with the shared backbone, requiring intermediate representations to support both early classification and subsequent feature refinement. Under joint training, the corresponding optimization objectives jointly update shared backbone parameters, which can lead to conflicting gradient directions. Motivated by this observation, we introduce DeclareViT, a framework that decouples early classification from feature refinement. Each exit uses a dedicated query to read intermediate features through one-way cross-attention without modifying the backbone token stream. The query branches are optimized for early classification while the backbone and final classifier remain frozen. Across ViT, DeiT, and Swin on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1K, and Food-101, DeclareViT consistently establishes a state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency trade-off: It achieves 1.58 times to 2.57 times multiply-accumulate (MAC)-based speed-up with only a 0.39-1.91 percentage-point accuracy drop. Wall-clock measurements on CPU and GPU further demonstrate practical inference acceleration. Code is available at https://github.com/TUDa-HWAI/DeclareViT.

candidates.title: An $n^{1/O(\log^* n)}$ Lower Bound for Online Coloring of $k$-Colorable Graphs
candidates.abstract: In online coloring, the vertices of a graph arrive one at a time with their edges to earlier vertices, and each vertex must be colored irrevocably on arrival. For graphs promised to be $k$-colorable, with $k\ge 3$ fixed, the best deterministic algorithms use $n^{1-Θ(1/k^2)}$ colors, while the best lower bound was Vishwanathan's $Ω(\log^{k-1}n)$ from 1990 until Li recently proved $2^{Ω((\log n)^{1/3}(\log\log n)^{2/3})}$. For every fixed $k\ge 3$ and all sufficiently large $n$, we prove a lower bound of $n^{1/(\log^*n+3)}$ colors for deterministic online algorithms on $n$-vertex $k$-colorable graphs, and the same lower bound in expectation for randomized online algorithms. Both bounds hold on a single triangle-free $3$-colorable graph: even an algorithm that is shown this graph in advance, but is not told which of its vertices each arriving vertex is, can be forced to use this many colors by a suitable arrival order. The hard instances are iterated blow-ups of a clique, in which every vertex becomes a block of independent vertices and every edge a private server in the earlier block; each blow-up keeps the forced colors and replaces the chromatic number $χ$ by about $\logχ$, so about $\log^*n$ blow-ups bring it down to $k$. We also show that deterministic lower bounds for different values of $k\ge 3$ are polynomially equivalent, and that no adversary presenting such iterated blow-ups can force more than $n^{1/(\log^*n-O(1))}$ colors. All numbered results are formalized in Lean 4.
candidates.comment: 45 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Lean 4 formalization and reproduction material: https://github.com/sfmqrb/lean-verifications-k-colorable

candidates.title: PROPS: Can Visual Generators Keep the Current Look of a Prop?
candidates.abstract: Many generation tasks draw the next image from a visual history, such as storyboards, illustrated stories and multi-turn editing. A new request often states what happens next without restating how earlier objects look. Instead of recovering an object's current look from the history, generators often redraw it from the request alone or bring back an outdated look, and the error can carry into later steps. We call this failure prop drift. Existing evaluations rarely isolate it, because similarity to the history rewards copying and a judge that sees a single history cannot tell a look recovered from that history from one the generator happens to prefer. We introduce PROPS, a benchmark of 2,257 pairs of twin histories that end on the same request but show one prop in two different looks. A pair passes only if the generator draws the matching look on each side and carries out the request, so a look preferred by the generator or the judge passes at most one side. All 34 open and closed systems we test show prop drift, and even systems that carry out the requested action on most sides often lose the current look of the prop. Swapping the planners and editors of agents further shows that both history understanding and image generation limit agent performance. We also build PROPS-Train, 80,250 training chains in four tracks whose targets recover an earlier state or carry scripted changes forward, and fine-tuning on it clearly improves all four tested models. Both datasets will be publicly released.

candidates.title: Position-Skipped Distillation of Sparse-Attention Indexers: Train Short, Serve Long
candidates.abstract: Top-k sparse attention relies on an indexer, a lightweight per-layer module that ranks cached tokens so attention covers only the k highest-scoring ones. Indexers are usually distilled from dense attention at the full serving length, so every training step pays for long-context dense attention. We show that when an indexer is distilled on short sequences, its failure to generalise to longer contexts is driven mainly by rotary positional encoding (RoPE), not by degraded content matching. We propose position-skipped distillation: the indexer and the frozen teacher see short sequences whose position IDs contain a randomly placed gap, so neither ever processes more than the short training length. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B, an indexer distilled on 8K tokens this way matches a 32K-distilled indexer to within about 0.5 perplexity up to 32K, and on DeepSeek-V2-Lite matches a 64K-distilled indexer at 64K with roughly 6x less training compute per token. On Llama-3.1-8B it trails the stronger 32K run by 0.6 perplexity, and at 64K simple position compression is often as good, so the main gain is training cost rather than quality. We also quantise indexer keys to 3-4 bits without retraining and score them with a fused integer kernel: at 4 bits, perplexity changes by at most 0.05 and the scan is 1.6-2.2x faster than half precision. In a current serving engine, the indexer speeds up decoding only for long contexts with multiple concurrent streams.

candidates.title: Exact on Paper: Which LLM Serving Shortcuts Flip Graded Answers, Measured Against the Noise of Reordering the Same Requests
candidates.abstract: Teams enable serving features such as prefix caching, chunked prefill and speculative decoding after checking that benchmark accuracy is unchanged, because the engine documents them as exact. Accuracy is an aggregate, so a feature can hold it while flipping which requests are answered correctly. We serve one 4B instruction model in vLLM under nine single feature configurations and five replicas of a reference configuration, grade 3,380 requests from five benchmarks in every run, and compare each candidate with a restart floor (fresh process) and a scheduling floor (same requests in a different order). With default kernels every configuration keeps accuracy within one point, and the seven exact features flip the graded outcome of 1.47% (95% CI 1.13 to 1.85) to 1.78% (1.39 to 2.20) of requests, none above the scheduling floor of 1.72%, while the FP8 KV cache flips 3.36% (2.80 to 3.96), as many as FP8 weights. With batch invariant kernels all seven exact features, speculative decoding included, reproduce the reference text on every request, while the FP8 KV cache still flips 3.91% (3.28 to 4.53) of graded outcomes. A gate that compares against a single replica pair rejected an unchanged configuration, so we recommend certifying a serving change under batch invariant kernels, where the floor is zero, or against a scheduling floor measured from at least three replicas.
candidates.comment: 8 pages, 2 figures. Also archived on Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.24433980

candidates.title: Grounded in Contact: Reducing Floating and Interpenetration Artifacts with Multimodal Skill-Effect Models
candidates.abstract: Learning to predict the effects of contact-rich manipulation skills requires models that represent distinct outcome modes rather than a single expected result. Even for basic skills such as pushing, picking, and placing, small variations in contact conditions or object geometry can produce qualitatively different object motions under nearly identical states and actions. Deterministic and Gaussian models tend to average over these alternatives or represent them as a single broad distribution, obscuring distinct modes such as sliding, toppling, and rotating. We study probabilistic skill-effect models that learn multimodal distributions over object pose changes given partial point clouds and actions. We instantiate this abstraction with three representative model classes: mixture density networks, state tokenization, and flow matching, each paired with latent dynamics for next-step prediction. Across diverse objects and skills, explicitly multimodal models predict which outcome occurs more accurately than deterministic and Gaussian baselines. In planning, flow matching significantly improves task success over the deterministic baseline on every skill and achieves the highest success on every multi-step sequence. On a real robot, probabilistic models succeed at pick about twice as often as the deterministic baseline, providing evidence that probabilistic skill effects offer a practical abstraction for reasoning and planning under uncertainty.
candidates.comment: Under review. Project page: https://grounded-in-contact.github.io/. The second and third authors contributed equally

candidates.title: One Checkpoint, Four Converters: Per Input Disagreement After On Device Conversion and a Probe Set That Catches It
candidates.abstract: A model converted for on device or accelerated inference ships once its top 1 accuracy matches the source model. Accuracy can match while individual decisions change, and the converter, its INT8 recipe and its calibration draw each move them. We convert 5 public checkpoints (four ImageNet classifiers and a sentiment model) with the documented FP32 and INT8 recipes of ExecuTorch, LiteRT, ONNX Runtime and TensorRT and compare every top 1 decision with the PyTorch source on 7,854 images and 1,938 sentences. All 34 strict FP32 conversions reproduce every decision, yet each of the 4 vision INT8 recipes that keeps accuracy equivalent flips more than 1% of decisions: ONNX Runtime static INT8 flips 4.07% (95% CI [3.65, 4.53]) of ResNet 50 decisions while accuracy moves by -0.15 points, and two builds of that recipe from different calibration draws disagree on 3.44% [3.06, 3.88]. Where accuracy is kept, the flipped inputs are the ones the source model barely decides (AUROC of the source margin 0.90 to 0.97 on ResNet 50, every 95% CI inside [0.89, 0.98]), but our preregistered claim that this holds for every recipe fails on the two mobile networks, where INT8 breaks accuracy outright. A probe set of the 200 training inputs with the smallest source margin, chosen before any conversion, flags all 40 vision stacks (recall 95% CI [0.91, 1.00]) and all 6 text stacks that flip at least 0.5% of decisions and none of the exact FP32 conversions, so conversion checks should compare decisions on such a probe set, not accuracy.
candidates.comment: 6 pages, 3 figures. Also archived on Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.24433993

candidates.title: Faster Directed SSSP on Digraphs with Random Sparse Supports or Few DFS Exceptions
candidates.abstract: We study exact single-source shortest paths (SSSP) in directed graphs with $n$ vertices, $m$ arcs and nonnegative real weights, in the comparison-addition model. This paper continues our earlier work, which gave a deterministic algorithm that takes $O(n\sqrt{\log n}(\log\log n)^{1/4})$ time when $m=O(n)$ and $O(n\sqrt{\log n}(\log\log n)^{5/8})$ time when $m=Θ(n\sqrt{\log\log n})$. Our two deterministic algorithms compute the distances on every input and take $O(n\sqrt{\log n})$ time on two families of inputs, one per density. The support of an input is its underlying simple undirected graph. When $m=O(n)$, the first algorithm takes $O(n\sqrt{\log n})$ time if no two simple cycles of the support with fewer than $P$ vertices share a vertex, where $P=Θ(\sqrt{\log n})$ depends only on the support. For fixed $c>0$, a uniformly random graph with $n$ vertices and $\lfloor cn\rfloor$ edges has this property with probability at least $1-n^{-1+o(1)}$, and the bound then holds for every choice of one or both directions of each edge, all weights and every source. The second family is defined through the depth-first search tree of the support that starts at the source and visits neighbours in identifier order. For fixed $k\ge1$, call a set $Y$ of exceptional vertices $k$-feasible if, for each nonroot vertex, at most $k$ of its proper ancestors are joined to its subtree by arcs whose endpoints avoid $Y$ and whose underlying edges lie outside the DFS tree. Given $k$ but not such a set, the second algorithm takes, for every $k$-feasible set $Y$ of total out-degree $d^+(Y)$, time $O_k(n+m+(1+|Y|)\log n+\sqrt{(n+m)d^+(Y)\log n})$. When $m=Θ(n\sqrt{\log\log n})$, this is $O_k(n\sqrt{\log n})$ if some $k$-feasible set has $O(n/\sqrt{\log n})$ vertices and total out-degree $O(n/\sqrt{\log\log n})$.

candidates.title: How Reliable is AI-Generated Audio Description? A Multilingual Expert Evaluation
candidates.abstract: Audio description (AD) makes visual media, such as video, accessible to blind or low-vision (BLV) audiences, but the high cost of professional production limits coverage. Due to recent advances in AI, numerous approaches to automatically generate intermediate AD scripts and/or final AD audios have been proposed. We present an expert evaluation of AI-generated AD scripts for movies in Italian and German that compares two AI systems, a GPT-4o- and a Qwen-based pipeline, against human-authored descriptions. Professional audio describers rated description quality and annotated errors using a detailed error taxonomy that includes content, character, fluency and coherence errors. The results show that while GPT-4o outperforms the Qwen models, both AI systems still fall short of human professional quality: the generated descriptions show substantially higher error rates and lower quality ratings. Based on the error annotations, we identify two key areas that require improvement: 1) character references, which includes both issues with identification and coherent naming, and 2) content errors and hallucinations, where the AD misrepresents or invents events. These error types are particularly critical, as they directly affect the viewer's ability to follow the narrative.

candidates.title: Scaled Relative Graph Separation for Unbounded Nonlinear Systems
candidates.abstract: We investigate stability analysis of one-channel nonlinear feedback systems based on the recent notion of scaled relative graph (SRG). Our focus is on the SRG separation in the complex plane for feedback stability analysis that involves possibly unbounded open-loop nonlinear systems. Subject to a technical assumption, a homotopy-based SRG separation theorem is developed as the main result, where the incremental directed gap is utilized as a key instrument to quantify robust feedback stability along the homotopy path. Doing so enables us to incorporate commonly used integrators as unbounded systems in the SRG-based framework. Specializations of the main result to linear systems, along with illustrative examples, are also provided to demonstrate its effectiveness.
candidates.comment: An extended version of a conference paper accepted for the 65th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control, 2026

candidates.title: Directed Hypergraphs: Tensor Representation, Embedding Modeling, and Community Detection
candidates.abstract: Directed hypergraphs, in which each hyperedge connects a set of tail nodes to a set of head nodes, are the natural representation for many-to-many interactions in citation networks, metabolic pathways, and group communications. Despite their broad applicability, community detection for directed hypergraphs remains statistically underdeveloped: most existing methods either collapse hyperedges into pairwise edges, treat the two sides as interchangeable, or require the number of communities to be known. We propose a statistical framework for simultaneous embedding and community detection in nonuniform directed hypergraphs. The method allows each node to have distinct roles as a source and as a target, accommodates varying hyperedge sizes, and automatically determines the unknown numbers of communities on both sides, which need not be equal, through a fusion-penalized likelihood. We establish consistency of the estimated numbers of communities, exact recovery of both membership structures, and consistent probability tensor estimation. We further show that exact recovery is attainable without knowing the numbers of communities by a procedure that does not rely on any particular local solution, and we complement the upper bounds with a minimax lower bound for probability tensor estimation and a necessary condition for exact recovery. To ground the methodology, we construct the Cross-Statistics Citation Network, a new large-scale corpus linking Statistics with Biology, Computer Science, and Economics. Applying our method to this corpus reveals source and target roles of author communities in cross-field knowledge flow, and a pairwise representation of the same citations partly merges these roles.

candidates.title: How Seasonal Reference Choice Changes the Apparent Gains of Chronos Models in Electricity Load Forecasting
candidates.abstract: When a forecasting model is said to beat a simple baseline, the size of that win depends on which baseline was used. We measure how much this matters for two zero-shot foundation models, Chronos-Bolt and Chronos-2, on hourly electricity load. The study uses 60 fixed cases drawn from eight series in four public collections, with forecasts 24 and 168 hours ahead and up to 2,048 hours of history. Each model is compared with daily persistence, weekly persistence, a weekday hybrid, a daily-weekly blend, and a reference chosen from these on a validation period. We keep every origin-level forecast and estimate uncertainty with paired circular block bootstrap intervals using 168- and 336-hour blocks. A week ahead, Bolt clearly beats weekly persistence in 21 of 30 cases but the validation-selected reference in only 14, and its median gain falls from 17.3% to 11.9%. For Chronos-2 the clear-win counts are 18 and 15. Chronos-2 has lower week-ahead MAE than Bolt in 24 cases, yet only 12 of those differences are clear. The selected reference is not always the harder baseline, since on some test windows it does worse than weekly persistence. The choice of baseline therefore changes both how large the reported gain is and how sure we can be of it. The results are exploratory: the series and windows are related, an earlier pilot was inspected, pretraining overlap cannot be ruled out, and the case-level intervals are not corrected for multiple comparisons.

candidates.title: Which Loopholes Get Found? Predicting Reward Hacking of LLM Judges Before RL Training
candidates.abstract: A policy trained against an LLM judge can learn to exploit its loopholes. Static probes show that such judges accept degenerate answers like a lone "{" or "Thought process:", but not which flaw a policy will find. In GRPO the first loophole to be exploited can be predicted before training from each pattern's exposure, the product of the starting policy's propensity to produce it and the judge's false-positive rate (FPR). To test exposure causally, we seed the patterns into fine-tuning at three doses in a Latin square. Across 36 GRPO runs with seven judges, the first exploited pattern had the highest exposure in all 12 runs with exploitation and the highest FPR in only 6. Predictions recorded before training held in three of four runs with one pattern masked by rule. When only two patterns were seeded, at 3% to 3.8% of the fine-tuning data and chosen so that exposure disagreed with FPR alone or propensity alone, exposure named the first exploited pattern and its onset window in all six runs. Exploitation occurred only on hard prompts, where an accepted exploit gets a large group-normalized advantage. Auditing exposure before RL therefore identifies the loophole a policy will likely exploit first.
candidates.comment: 16 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. Code and run summaries: https://github.com/justLxy/which-loopholes-get-found

candidates.title: JKO-GRPO: Augmenting GRPO with Wasserstein Proximal Steps for Flow-Matching VLAs
candidates.abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $π_0,π_{0.5}$ generate continuous action chunks by flow matching, and online reinforcement learning (RL) can improve them beyond supervised fine-tuning. Existing methods, such as Flow-GRPO and $π_{\mathrm{RL}}$, optimize likelihood ratios of stochastic denoising transitions, which reweight the sampled actions by their advantages but do not use the distances between them. We propose JKO-GRPO, which augments Flow-GRPO with Wasserstein proximal steps, with two contributions: (1) At each state, we treat the group of sampled actions as an empirical distribution and formulate policy improvement as a Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) step. We use a soft discrete $c$-transform to construct transport targets from group-relative advantages and combine shared-noise regression of the deterministic flow sampler onto these targets and combined with the clipped Flow-GRPO objective without Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization. (2) We extend this approach to sequential VLA control through random-time branching: we select one or multiple action-chunk indices along old-policy trajectories and independently apply group-level JKO updates using candidate continuations from the corresponding states.

candidates.title: Reducing Authorship Attribution Risk in Student Texts Through Style-Conditioned Rewriting
candidates.abstract: Building NLP applications for education is constrained by data scarcity due to student privacy concerns and data regulations. To address this, we propose a style-aware approach to rewriting student forum posts that retains analytical value while reducing identifiability. Our method isolates content, structure, and style as separate conditioning channels and aggregates over student-disjoint exemplar partitions within style clusters, extending Differentially Private In-context Learning (DP-ICL) with cluster-restricted retrieval. Across three educational NLP datasets, our approach achieves high style fidelity, preserves downstream task performance, and reduces authorship attribution risk relative to the original student-written texts, including against a dedicated authorship-attribution model.

candidates.title: Group Buying through Bankruptcy Rules: Cost Sharing and Endogenous Pricing
candidates.abstract: Group buying allows independent buyers to pool their demand and benefit from quantity discounts that would not be available to them individually. While collective purchasing reduces total procurement costs, it raises a fundamental allocation question: how should the resulting savings be distributed among heterogeneous buyers? We address this question by integrating cost-allocation and bankruptcy approaches into a unified group-buying framework. Starting from a continuous quantity discount function, we examine cost-gap-based allocation mechanisms and develop an endogenous pricing representation in which each buyer's effective discount may depend on the demand profile of the entire group. We then establish a connection between group buying and bankruptcy theory by interpreting the aggregate savings from cooperation as the estate and each buyer's potential savings as its claim. This formulation allows us to derive cost-allocation mechanisms based on the proportional, constrained equal awards, constrained equal losses, and Talmud rules. For each rule, we obtain the corresponding buyer-specific price function and characterize the associated variable discount factor. We further examine the relationships between bankruptcy-based and cost-gap-based allocation mechanisms and use a numerical example with simulated data to compare their implications. The proposed framework links alternative fairness principles for allocating cooperative savings to economically interpretable pricing mechanisms, providing a unified basis for analyzing how group purchasing gains are distributed among heterogeneous buyers.

candidates.title: TASC: Time-to-Collision Anticipation and Selective Crowd Attention for Non-Holonomic Service Robots
candidates.abstract: Service robots that share corridors and lobbies with people must keep moving without endangering them. Reactive planners can stop indefinitely in dense crowds (the freezing robot problem), whereas the attention-based learned navigators that dominate the standard crowd benchmark assume holonomic motion or emit discrete actions unsuited to a differential-drive base. This paper presents TASC, a navigation system for a non-holonomic service robot that integrates an attention-based crowd encoder, an anticipatory collision feature, and a continuous-control policy. We adapt the dual-selection attention module, originally developed for discrete-action value learning, to proximal policy optimization for continuous velocity control, and add a closing-speed time-to-collision feature, a conservative estimate of the time to contact that serves as both an observation and a reward term. The policy is trained on a high-fidelity 3D robot model in NVIDIA Isaac Lab with 10,000 parallel environments, social-force-model pedestrians, and randomized crowd sizes. In 30,000 evaluation episodes, each run to its end, the policy timed out in fewer than 0.5% at every tested crowd density. This liveness comes at a cost: pedestrian collisions rise from 4.5% with five pedestrians to 17.4% with ten. In an ablation with four seeds per variant, policies retrained without the time-to-collision feature succeed 4 to 7 percentage points less often. The policy runs in Gazebo without retraining and on a commercial differential-drive service robot through a ROS 2 package with an inference latency below 10 ms, verified in a hardware-in-the-loop test with virtual pedestrians.
candidates.comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Accepted for publication at the 2027 IEEE/SICE International Symposium on System Integration (SII)

candidates.title: Diversity in Unity, Theory in Practice: Hierarchical Multitask Benchmarks for Chinese Minority Languages
candidates.abstract: Despite the rapid advancement of LLMs, their performance on linguistically and culturally diverse minority languages within a unified national context remains underexplored. We present CMiLBench, a collection of hierarchical multitask benchmarks designed to translate theoretical notions of "diversity in unity" into practical evaluation for three representative Chinese minority languages: Tibetan, Mongolian, and Uyghur. CMiLBench comprises 24,663 instances across 5 difficulty levels and 17 tasks spanning foundational ability, cultural specificity, and safety alignment. We adopt existing dataset adaptation, minority knowledge construction, and high-resource benchmark translation to construct CMiLBench. We assess 14 state-of-the-art commercial and open-source LLMs with a hybrid framework that integrates automatic metrics and LLM-as-a-Judge scoring. The comparative experimental results reveal the gap between theoretical capability and practical utility. CMiLBench serves as a foundational and scalable evaluation resource to bridge the digital language divide and promote the informatization and intelligentization of low-resource Chinese minority languages.
candidates.journal_ref: Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers) (ACL 2026)

candidates.title: SuperFine3D: Efficient Global-Local Recursive Refinement for Extremely Detailed 3D Geometry Generation
candidates.abstract: High-resolution images contain rich visual details that require fine geometric structures for faithful 3D reconstruction. However, generating extremely detailed 3D geometry from images requires substantial computational resources and training data, making high-resolution geometry generation challenging for existing state-of-the-art models. In this paper, we present SuperFine3D, an efficient framework for generating extremely detailed 3D geometry through global-local recursive refinement. SuperFine3D learns a shared refinement operator from paired coarse-to-fine representations and recursively reuses it to progressively synthesize finer geometry beyond the training resolutions, without requiring additional paired supervision at target resolutions. To make recursive refinement computationally efficient, we introduce spatial-cell attention, which restricts high-resolution interactions to local spatial neighborhoods while maintaining bounded communication across neighboring cells. We further propose spatially anchored cross-scale guidance, which leverages globally contextualized coarse geometry to guide local detail synthesis and preserve structural consistency. In addition, geometry-aware training objectives encourage the refinement process to preserve stable geometric structures while introducing fine-grained surface details. Experiments demonstrate that SuperFine3D generates geometry at a $4096^3$ decoder-grid resolution, corresponding to a sparse $256^3$ latent lattice, using a shared refinement operator trained only on $512^3$--$1024^3$ representations. Compared with a full-attention recursive baseline, SuperFine3D achieves a $9.4\times$ speedup in end-to-end inference and reduces peak GPU memory usage by $23.0\%$, while improving cross-scale structural consistency and producing cleaner surfaces with finer geometric details.

candidates.title: Contamination at the Operating Point: Train-Test Identity Overlap Inflates Low-FMR Face Recognition Accuracy by an Order of Magnitude
candidates.abstract: Face verification systems are deployed by selecting a decision threshold that achieves a target false match rate (FMR); performance is then reported as the corresponding false non-match rate (FNMR). In practice, deployed systems operate at FMR $\le 10^{-6}$, but widely used benchmarks can share identities with the models' training corpora. Prior work (Wu et al., 2024) measures the resulting optimistic bias as a small additive change in 10-fold accuracy (up to 1.01 percentage points). We show that the bias is neither small nor constant: it is a multiplicative error that grows as FMR falls. First, we audit train-test overlap with a detector calibrated against a null distribution (rather than a hand-tuned threshold). Relative to WebFace42M, we flag 88.6% of MS1MV3 identities and 14.3% of IJB-C subjects as present, despite WebFace260M's published de-overlap explicitly naming IJB-C. Manual review of 100 flagged IJB-C subjects confirms 69.2%, implying a residual overlap of roughly 9.9%. Second, holding the model fixed, removing only the contaminated identities from the test set increases FNMR by 3.6$\times$ at FMR=$10^{-4}$, 6.3$\times$ at FMR=$10^{-5}$, and 13.9$\times$ at FMR=$10^{-6}$, while a same-size random removal does not. The effect is traced to a shorter impostor tail that lowers the threshold. The magnitude of the shift depends on the training corpus and does not cancel betweent margin between our model and a publicbaseline by half. Third, we give the first direct measurement of the effective number of independent impostor comparisons in IJB-C: only 2.7 million effectively independent comparisons at FMR=$10^{-6}$, which is below all commonly accepted reporting rules. Finallyth a known training corpus, we build areal-face protocol with audited zero overlap that resolves FMR=$10^{-8}$.

candidates.title: Explainable Emotion and Mental Health Reasoning in Large Language Models Using Theories of Emotion
candidates.abstract: Advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled a wide range of applications. However, their ability to simulate human-like behavior and reasoning remains unclear. While emotion detection is a better-established Natural Language Processing (NLP) task, existing approaches primarily focus on directly classifying text into predefined emotion classes, often overlooking the appraisal process that explains why an individual experiences a particular emotion in a given situation. In this work, we propose Psychology-based Chain-of-Thought (PsyCoT) reasoning, a theory-driven prompting strategy grounded in the Schachter-Singer and Cognitive Appraisal theories of emotion. We propose and evaluate PsyCoT for subjective NLP tasks, including emotion analysis, emotion intensity prediction, stress analysis, and depression severity identification. Our evaluation covers four levels of classification complexity: binary, multiclass, multi-label, and ordinal scaling, spanning 11 languages. We assess the performance of five state-of-the-art LLMs across these selected subjective NLP tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that PsyCoT prompt variants improve the standard chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting across the evaluated tasks. Across all evaluated tasks, PsyCoT yields F1 score gains ranging from 0.5% to 28.1%, depending on the model, task, and language configuration.

candidates.title: Attacking Tabular Foundation Models: An Experimental Taxonomy of Context Poisoning and Test-Time Evasion
candidates.abstract: Tabular foundation models condition predictions on labeled examples supplied at inference time, creating an attack surface that differs from conventional model training. We study four manipulation families (label flipping, backdoor context poisoning, clean-label context selection, and test-time evasion) and organize them by attack stage, label consistency, and distributional realism. TabPFN-2.5, TabICL, and XGBoost are evaluated on CIC-IDS2017 and N-BaIoT using a common preprocessing and evaluation pipeline. Backdoor context poisoning provides strong targeted control over the in-context models with little change in clean accuracy, whereas selecting real, correctly labeled boundary-crowding rows causes no systematic accuracy degradation up to a 20% bias fraction. A simplified surrogate-transfer constrained PGD attack inspired by, but not equivalent to, CAPGD also produces test-time evasion, outperforming equal-budget random noise in most settings. The comparison shows that attack effectiveness depends strongly on both where manipulation occurs and how much freedom the attacker has to alter the data.

candidates.title: Asymptotically Optimal Representation of Tree-Like Graphs
candidates.abstract: We show how to represent a graph with $n$ nodes, $m=n+k=O(n)$ edges, and $h\le k$ nodes with more than one incoming edge in asymptotically optimal space, in a way that supports basic navigational operations quickly.

candidates.title: Randomized MST Certification beyond Cacti
candidates.abstract: We study minimum spanning tree certification under explorable edge uncertainty. Edge weights lie in open intervals or singleton sets, and querying an edge reveals its weight at a known positive cost. On general graphs the best known randomized competitive ratio is $1+1/\sqrt2$, while the optimal ratio $3/2$ is known only for cacti. We go beyond cacti in two ways, with conditions that refer to the uncertain edges outside the upper-limit tree rather than to the graph alone. For unit query costs we give a $3/2$-competitive algorithm, which is best possible, whenever every block has at most two such edges; this includes all graphs whose blocks are cycles or theta graphs. The algorithm replaces the constant budget of the water-filling method by budgets chosen with lookahead to the next fundamental cycle. For arbitrary positive query costs and every fixed $k\ge1$, we obtain ratio $1+\sqrt{k/(2(k+1))}$ whenever every block has at most $k$ such edges, in particular when every block has cycle rank at most $k$. This is below $1+1/\sqrt2$ for every $k$, and we show that it is the best ratio attainable with a constant water-filling budget.

candidates.title: Wactorz: Self-Writing LLM Agents That Discover, Repair, and Migrate at the Edge
candidates.abstract: Most LLM agent frameworks build a crew that runs a task and exits. Physical environments (e.g., homes, labs, factory floors) need agents that stay up for months, survive their own bugs, and run on whatever hardware is already next to the sensors. We present Wactorz, an open-source runtime in which LLM-generated agents are long-lived, supervised actors: a planner turns a chat request into Python, compiles it into a new actor at runtime, and a supervisor restarts that actor alone, with its state intact, when it crashes. All coordination rides on MQTT, so agents can be spawned on, and live-migrated between, edge nodes such as a Raspberry Pi, and every internal event is a topic external systems can subscribe to. The recorded demo builds a camera-to-lamp automation from one chat request, adds a second agent that is auto-wired to the first by topic and carries a deliberate division-by-zero, watches that agent repair its own code without losing its count, then deploys a fresh Raspberry Pi node and live-migrates the agent onto it, in under four minutes of wall-clock time and \$0.13 of model usage. This extended version adds what the two-page demonstration paper could not: the Wiring view of the topic graph, Wactorz as a library for hand-written agents, how trained models are stored, sent to nodes and replaced, the security model, and the system's limitations.
candidates.comment: 5 pages. 2 figues. Extended version of a paper accepted to the AAAI-27 Demonstrations Program. Code: https://github.com/waldiez/wactorz

candidates.title: Mass Forcing: On-Policy Mass-Aware Distillation for Autoregressive Video Generation
candidates.abstract: Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) has emerged as a promising paradigm for real-time video synthesis, distilling pretrained diffusion models into few-step autoregressive generators. However, its reverse-KL objective is mode-seeking and can collapse the student's conditional video distribution onto a narrow subset of modes, leading to reduced sample diversity, diminished temporal dynamics, and color oversaturation. Existing methods mitigate this issue mainly via coverage-oriented student initialization, but we observe that such coverage is transient: across three initializations, the fraction of dynamic videos drops sharply during subsequent DMD training, indicating that the mode-seeking objective, not the initialization, drives this degradation. We propose Mass Forcing, a probability-mass-aware framework that moves on-policy DMD supervision from whole videos to individual states. Each update branches several continuations from a shared student-generated prefix, making the student's probability mass at that state measurable against the teacher. First, Mass Forcing estimates relative teacher-to-student density ratios among these continuations through latent-space score integration and uses them to rebalance conditional DMD updates, amplifying rollouts underrepresented relative to the teacher. Second, since mismatched mode probabilities do not necessarily induce strong local score corrections, it aligns generated rollout sets with a reweighted reference distribution defined by the same mass estimates, providing cross-rollout supervision. Experiments on MovieGen and VBench show that Mass Forcing improves video fidelity and sustains temporal dynamics throughout training, achieving the highest Total scores among compared methods and a Dynamic Degree of 83% after 1,000 generator updates, versus 12-32% for the baselines, with no additional inference-time overhead.

candidates.title: Tightness of the Partition Bound for Multiterminal Secret Key Capacity
candidates.abstract: We consider secret key agreement among \(m\) terminals, each observing one component of a finite-alphabet discrete memoryless multiple source. The terminals communicate over a noiseless public channel, and a target set \(A\subseteq[m]\) seeks to generate a shared secret key, with the remaining terminals acting as helpers. The partition-based Csiszár--Narayan upper bound on secret key capacity is known to be tight without helpers but can be strict in their presence. We give a complete characterization of its tightness: for \(2\leq |A|\leq m\), the bound is tight for every source if and only if \(|A|\in\{2,m-2,m-1,m\}\). To prove tightness, we use the supermodularity of conditional entropy and the structure of optimal supports in the linear program for communication for omniscience. We first establish the result under strict supermodularity and then remove this assumption by a perturbation argument. For all remaining pairs \((m,|A|)\), we extend Chan's six-terminal counterexample. We also study optimal partitions when there are two target terminals and the source is a Markov random field on a connected graph. We show that an optimal bipartition separating the targets can be chosen so that both blocks induce connected subgraphs. For cycles, this reduces the number of candidate bipartitions from exponential to at most quadratic in \(m\).

candidates.title: GravHMR: Coupling SLAM and Human Mesh Recovery in a Shared Gravity Frame
candidates.abstract: Recovering globally consistent 3D human motion from monocular videos remains challenging under dynamic camera motion. Although SLAM and human mesh recovery (HMR) provide complementary camera and body estimates, directly combining them often leads to inconsistent orientations and accumulated trajectory drift. We present GravHMR, a training-free, plug-and-play framework that couples SLAM and HMR through a shared gravity-aligned reference. By allowing gravity to be estimated independently of the HMR backbone, GravHMR accommodates world-grounded HMR models with or without explicit gravity-view representations. Specifically, Yaw-Aware Orientation Optimization (YAOO) resolves heading inconsistencies by correcting body and velocity orientations about the shared gravity axis. Conditioned on these corrected orientations, Gravity-Aware Trajectory Optimization (GATO) anchors root trajectories in the metric SLAM world by jointly leveraging 2D reprojection, the metric scale implicit in the human body, and the body's own motion. On EMDB-2, GravHMR achieves state-of-the-art performance with 154.0 mm W-MPJPE100 using ViPE and 189.8 mm using masked DROID-SLAM, outperforming TRAM (222.4 mm) under the same masked DROID-SLAM camera estimates. It further reduces W-MPJPE100 by 44.3% over GVHMR (276.5 mm) and by 20.0% over GVHMR + HTD-Refine (192.4 mm) with the same HMR backbone.

candidates.title: Weight Coding: Evolving Web-Scale Recommenders through Direct Weight Edits with LLM Agents
candidates.abstract: Web-scale recommender models evolve primarily through retraining or fine-tuning. We propose \emph{weight coding}, a methodology for model evolution through direct, executable weight edits. A large language model (LLM) agent inspects model structure and parameters, formulates hypotheses, and implements edits using evaluation feedback. The loop progresses from localized changes to targeted searches and composition, allowing edited components to adapt to one another. A cached engine enables rapid forward evaluation without backpropagation. On Pinterest's 147M-parameter Image Search two-tower retriever, weight coding improves held-out recall@10 of production model by up to 15.0 percentage points (+24\% relative) with few edits in about 1/4 GPU hours of a full post-training finetune, while a common launch only improves around 1\%. After reinitializing the entire 13.6M-parameter interaction module randomly while retaining the surrounding trained model, searching 2,448 mixing and normalization parameters yields 9.8 points above production. Offline gains span the full funnel including dense retrieval, generative retrieval and ranking, with up to 1.37B learnable parameters and different edits for each architecture. Steering edits provide explicit control of model performance over segments like freshness and product. Weight coding requires no serving change and online A/B tests increase saves per user from the edited retrieval source by 8.4\% to 10.7\%, aligned with the target business objectives. Our results establish weight coding as a practical and useful tool for model development and and behavioral control in a real web-scale production system, with potential to extend to both pre-training and post-training stages across the funnel.

candidates.title: Dr. Grasp-RL: Diverse and Robust Dexterous Grasping via Reinforcement Learning
candidates.abstract: Human interaction with physical objects relies on a combination of dexterity and robustness. In robotic manipulation, dexterity requires not only flexible end effectors but also a diverse repertoire of manipulation strategies, while robustness requires closed-loop adaptation to disturbances and unexpected situations. Two prominent research directions in dexterous grasping have largely addressed these capabilities separately. Generative approaches model multimodal distributions to produce diverse grasp poses, but their reliance on open-loop execution can limit robustness. Reinforcement learning approaches learn closed-loop grasping policies, but can converge to a narrow range of successful grasping strategies, limiting behavioral diversity. We introduce a time-reversed curriculum with a coordinated reset mechanism that enables a simple MLP policy trained with PPO to capture multiple modes of the grasp-pose distribution while maintaining closed-loop control. Experiments demonstrate both diverse grasping behaviors and robust closed-loop execution. Trained on only approximately 400 objects, our policy further demonstrates strong generalization when evaluated on more than 20,000 unseen objects.

candidates.title: JEPA-Shield: Safe Diffusion Planning with Latent World Models via Conformal Shielding
candidates.abstract: Latent world models enable planning from images, but their predictions do not directly establish whether a robot will satisfy physical constraints. We present JEPA-Shield, which connects a frozen action-conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world model to task-space safety enforcement. Two downstream models predict relative motion from imagined latent rollouts and decode unsafe geometry from the current image. Split conformal prediction turns end-to-end motion-prediction errors into multi-horizon uncertainty tubes. A backup-based shield checks these tubes against physical constraints and screens both candidate trajectories and final proposals in diffusion-inspired sampling-based model predictive control. Under the stated exchangeability and initial-backup assumptions, we establish probabilistic constraint satisfaction at action-block boundaries for a returned plan executed without replanning. We also introduce VParkBench, with geometric car and tractor-trailer parking tasks and a editable photorealistic Gaussian-splatting environment. In closed-loop evaluation, JEPA-Shield achieves success rates of 84.4%, 82.3%, and 99.0%, respectively, with no observed constraint violations. Ablations show complementary benefits from shielding and uncertainty calibration. The results demonstrate the importance of grounding latent world-model predictions in task-space quantities and explicitly accounting for prediction uncertainty in safety-critical planning.

candidates.title: Aggregation Dispersion: An Information-Geometric Diagnostic of Oversmoothing in Graph Neural Networks
candidates.abstract: Message-passing neural networks (MPNNs) learn node representations by iteratively aggregating information from neighbors, but stacking too many layers causes all representations to converge, an effect known as oversmoothing. We propose a geometric perspective on this phenomenon. At each depth $k$, the propagation operator assigns to every node $v$ a walk distribution $p_v^{(k)}$, a probability distribution over source nodes. These walk distributions form a point cloud on the probability simplex, whose contraction to a single point characterizes complete mixing of the propagation operator, and thus oversmoothing. To measure this contraction, we use the Fisher-Rao metric, the unique Riemannian metric on the simplex invariant up to scale under sufficient statistics, whose scaled chordal distance under the square-root embedding $p \mapsto \sqrt{p}$ is the Hellinger distance. The resulting diagnostic, the aggregation dispersion $D_k$, is the variance of the embedded point cloud on the unit sphere. We prove that: (i) $D_k = 0$ if and only if the $k$-th step propagation matrix has rank one, a necessary and sufficient condition for complete operator mixing; (ii) $D_k$ is non-increasing with depth; (iii) the spectral gap of the propagation matrix controls the rate of this decay; and (iv) for contractive MPNNs, the aggregation dispersion upper-bounds the representation dispersion up to graph- and initialization-dependent constants. Across 14 model configurations and 11 datasets, $D_k$ attains the highest mean absolute Pearson correlation with test accuracy across depths among eight diagnostics ($|r| = 0.721$, using log-transformed diagnostic values), numerically comparable to the post-training effective rank ($|r| = 0.688$), while requiring no training.
candidates.comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

candidates.title: AEP:Towards Trustworthy Agent Communication, Networking, and Collaboration
candidates.abstract: As privately owned agents become increasingly capable, collaboration in open agent networks is limited by partial topology knowledge, ownership boundaries, and the risk of exposing or contaminating private context. Existing agent-to-agent protocols are useful when collaborators are already known, while shared-memory and broadcast-based systems rely on visibility and trust assumptions that do not hold in decentralized, low-trust environments. We introduce Open Private Agent Collaboration (OPAC), an asset-centric paradigm for cooperation among private agents with open membership, partial observability, and ownership-aware access control. Rather than treating collaboration as the exchange of final responses, OPAC enables agents to selectively discover, exchange, audit, and integrate policy-controlled context assets. This shifts the unit of cooperation from transient messages to reusable external context, while keeping disclosure and integration subject to privacy and security constraints. We instantiate OPAC with the Agent Exchange Protocol (AEP), a decentralized framework that combines semantic discovery, demand-driven coordination, safety-gated asset exchange, and ledger-backed evidence derivation. By distinguishing physical topology from each agent's local cognitive topology, AEP allows agents to discover task-conditioned collaborators under an unknown network structure, release only admissible assets, and update future cooperation decisions from auditable interaction evidence. AEP therefore provides a middle ground between pure request-response interaction and globally shared memory, offering a practical foundation for trustworthy agent-native networking through selective, auditable reuse of distributed context assets.

candidates.title: Similarity-Constrained Reweighting for Complex Query Answering on Knowledge Graphs
candidates.abstract: Machine learning models for Complex Query Answering (CQA) on knowledge graphs estimate the likelihood of answers that are not reachable via direct traversal. Recent work has proposed extending such queries with soft entity constraints, which require the target variable to be similar or dissimilar to specified sets of entities. We study a more general formulation where similarity constraints are specified on an arbitrary variable in a query, and introduce SCORE: a computationally efficient and interpretable method for incorporating similarity constraints on an arbitrary variable of a query. SCORE is based on a lightweight and interpretable score adjustment function that only requires tuning two hyperparameters on a validation set. Our experiments show that SCORE effectively incorporates preferences while maintaining strong query answering performance. It significantly improves ranking quality when constraints apply to the target variable and performs effectively in the more general case involving constraints on intermediate variables, and its performance remains robust when applied to several existing methods for CQA. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/dfdazac/score.

candidates.title: Rethinking Closed-Ended Medical VLM Evaluation: From Stable Wrongness to Counterfactual Answer Sensitivity
candidates.abstract: As medical VLMs are increasingly evaluated for clinical decision-support scenarios, knowing when to trust their predictions is critical. Closed-ended medical VQA has become a common benchmark format because it enables automated scoring. Yet, systematic investigation into whether this format changes the reliability problem remains scarce. We identify a failure mode that we call stable wrongness: models can produce incorrect yes/no answers that remain confident and repeatable even when patient-specific visual evidence is removed or mismatched. This failure violates the premise behind sampling-stability uncertainty methods, including recent hallucination-aware calibration (HAC) variants: disagreement is informative only when errors are unstable. When shortcut-driven errors are themselves stable, sampling agreement can remain deceptively high. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce Counterfactual Answer Sensitivity (CAS), which shifts reliability estimation from answer stability to evidence sensitivity. CAS uses cross-modal counterfactual interventions, such as text-only, black, and corrupted images, to audit whether a committed yes/no answer remains supported when visual evidence is invalidated. Across 7 VLMs and 3 benchmarks, CAS outperforms the best HAC-family scores across all evaluated settings, achieving a macro-averaged AUROC gain of +0.150 for error detection. Mechanistic analysis further shows that CAS recovers hidden errors in the HAC-confident region and that its strongest standalone signal is counterfactual decision-boundary shift rather than hard prediction stability. Our findings suggest that closed-ended evaluation should test visual dependence, not only answer stability, in safety-critical medical contexts.

candidates.title: KernelShift: Benchmarking Kernel Optimization Across Evolving Hardware
candidates.abstract: Efficient AI computation depends on hardware that evolves over time, shifting the strategies needed to implement performant code. For CPU kernels, a key evolving factor is the set of available architectural extensions, which expose specialized hardware instructions that change the techniques used to optimize kernels. We study how effectively coding agents use these new, potentially unfamiliar extensions to write fast code. We introduce KernelShift, a benchmarking pipeline and a set of environments for evaluating coding agents in kernel optimization across evolving CPU architectures. Its agent-assisted, human-verified pipeline turns code repositories into benchmark instances, and its environments let agents optimize code with feedback from the target hardware. Using this pipeline, we construct 99 kernels from real-world, actively developed repositories (ncnn, llama.cpp, Arm SIMD Loops, and KleidiAI), including inference workloads derived from real model executions. KernelShift supports incorporating new kernels and hardware configurations as libraries and processors evolve. We evaluate agents with proprietary and open-weight models across progressively newer architectural extensions (Arm Neon, SVE, SVE2, and SME2), examining how performance changes as hardware evolves. On established extensions, agents beat the auto-vectorized compiler everywhere (2.4-19.8x) and exceed general-purpose libraries such as ncnn (getting up to 2.74x over its Neon kernels), but fall behind Arm's hand-tuned KleidiAI kernels (0.70x). In end-to-end inference of two LLMs, agent-written kernels achieve a 1.3-1.6x prefill speedup over llama.cpp's fast path. However, current agents do not yet reliably adapt to new extensions that require unfamiliar programming models, such as SME2's matrix tiles.
candidates.comment: 26 pages, 9 figures, 22 tables. Project page: https://cmu-l3.github.io/kernel-shift/

candidates.title: Scalar Tuned Lens Summaries Offer Limited Incremental Value for Mid-Generation Abstention
candidates.abstract: Mid-generation abstention aims to stop an unpromising response before spending its remaining computation budget. Intermediate transformer states may help predict eventual correctness, but whether scalar summaries of their vocabulary predictions add useful evidence is less clear. We compare Tuned Lens entropy and divergence features with final-state and raw intermediate-state probes under matched, causal evaluation. Across eight instruction-tuned models on MATH-500, raw intermediate states improve ranking, whereas scalar-only probes usually trail the final-state baseline. Scalar hybrids have positive exceptions, but their advantage over position-matched permutation controls is small. Cross-fitted residual comparisons further show that gains over a final-state probe need not require aligned scalar features. Actual stopping runs on two model sizes and two benchmarks reveal a separate accuracy--computation trade-off, with token savings overstating wall-time savings for scalar policies. The evidence supports a restricted empirical conclusion about these scalar features, not a general negative claim about intermediate representations.

candidates.title: How Multi-Timescale Memory Cools Optimization: Theory and Evidence from AdEMAMix
candidates.abstract: Augmenting AdamW with multiple momentum timescales improves large language model pretraining, yet the mechanism driving these gains remains poorly understood. We identify an interaction between multi-timescale optimizer memory and the geometry of normalized networks: memory changes parameter norms and thereby controls how fast parameters rotate. Starting from exact norm dynamics under decoupled weight decay, we show that the parameter norm depends on the temporal correlation of the updates, with weight decay controlling how long these correlations influence optimization. We show how an independently weighted slow momentum can substantially increase the norm of parameters, while contributing negligible power to the instantaneous update, therefore acting as an endogenous annealing schedule. We study this mechanism in AdEMAMix for language-model pretraining. Controlled interventions show that this scheduling mechanism has clear practical consequences and is an important factor behind AdEMAMix's advantage over AdamW.

candidates.title: Feed-Forward Dimension Control for High-Dimensional Quantum Key Distribution over Time-Varying Airborne Free-Space Links
candidates.abstract: High-dimensional quantum key distribution tolerates more noise than qubit-based protocols, but the dimension that maximizes the secret key depends on turbulence, background light, device imperfections, and block size, all of which change during an airborne or satellite pass. Finite-size security analyses of high-dimensional protocols fix the dimension in advance, and the dimension-adaptive schemes reported so far have been analyzed only asymptotically. Here, a controller sets the dimension, acceptance thresholds, and key length of each block using only public data from earlier blocks. Each block is therefore a standard fixed-length protocol, and composable finite-key security against coherent attacks follows from sequential composition; an inaccurate channel model reduces the key rate but does not weaken security. The controller estimates turbulence from observed error rates, maximizes the expected key under forecast uncertainty, and recalibrates its model online. We evaluate it on a simulated entanglement-based orbital-angular-momentum link between an aircraft and a ground station, using Kolmogorov phase screens and the Hufnagel--Valley turbulence profile. Accounting for forecast uncertainty increases the key by 31\%--47\% relative to a naive planner. Over night, dawn, daytime, and model-mismatch scenarios, the recalibrated controller retains at least 98.8\% of the key obtained with the best fixed dimension for each scenario, while every fixed dimension drops to 73.5\% or less in at least one scenario. Running the link's measurement statistics on a superconducting quantum processor shows device errors close to a constant offset; with these errors included, the best daytime dimension changes from eight to four, and the controller adjusts accordingly.

candidates.title: LLM-Assisted Co-Optimization of RTL and Synthesis Algorithms via Bottleneck Analysis
candidates.abstract: Post-synthesis power, performance, and area (PPA) depend jointly on the register-transfer-level (RTL) code and the synthesis algorithms. However, the benefits of RTL optimization may be limited by bottlenecks in synthesis algorithms, and vice versa, leaving opportunities for better PPA unexplored by methods that optimize either level alone. In this work, we present a large language model (LLM)-assisted framework for regional co-optimization of RTL and synthesis algorithms via bottleneck analysis. A key insight behind our approach is that RTL structures and the Boolean networks used in synthesis expose complementary opportunities for addressing bottlenecks that lead to suboptimal PPA in different regions of the circuit. Our bottleneck analysis uses a Gaussian process (GP) to assess whether optimizing RTL or synthesis algorithms is more promising for each region. The GP learns from regional graph representations and PPA feedback. Using the GP's predictions and predictive uncertainty, Bayesian optimization (BO) provides guidance that an LLM Router combines with circuit analysis to choose how to address each region's bottlenecks. Self-improving LLM workers then optimize the RTL or synthesis algorithms in their assigned regions, and their regional changes are greedily integrated into the current design configuration. Experiments on 16 RTL designs show average improvements of 103.27% in worst negative slack (WNS), 1.23% in area, and 13.26% in power relative to the initial designs. These improvements exceed those of the strongest baseline for each metric by 47.80, 2.75, and 13.17 percentage points, respectively.

candidates.title: Social Interaction Breaks Replicate Independence in Controlled-Clone LLM Agents
candidates.abstract: Multi-agent LLM evaluations and social simulations create many agents from one model and treat them as independent replicates, even after the agents interact. This assumption remains untested with matched controls. We introduce SocCogEval, a controlled-clone assay for Social Cognitive Transfer (SCT). Clones share the base model, system prompt, and decoding parameters and differ only in a private brief, and a factorial protocol separates the brief, 30 rounds of interaction, and initialization noise. On Qwen3-122B-FP8, interaction with the briefs held fixed raises off-topic BFI-10 response-profile drift by $\barΔ=+0.917$ and $+0.912$ in two topically disjoint scenarios (exact $p=0.0008$ and $0.0039$). The drift is larger than under the brief alone, persists under temperature-zero re-probing, and stays positive without typed memory extraction in exploratory tests. Matched solo generation reproduces part of it, and social interaction remains highest. Across five more model variants, every scenario-averaged interaction contrast is positive. Each interacting population is therefore one replicate, and treating its agents as independent requires paired no-interaction controls.

candidates.title: From Learning Rates to Rotational Schedules: Finite-Horizon Theory on the Sphere
candidates.abstract: How should step sizes be scheduled across a finite training horizon? Cosine and warmup-stable-decay (WSD) schedules are widely adopted in large-scale pretraining, yet their effect on optimization also depends on parameter norms. Normalization can make parameter groups scale invariant, so that the loss depends only on their direction, while their norms still affect how fast the parameters rotate. In this work, we formulate schedule design directly in the space of rotational motion. Working within a geodesically convex spherical setting, we derive a last-iterate convergence guarantee for arbitrary rotational schedules that separates their overall scale from their distribution over time. We derive the unique schedule that minimizes this bound and prove that it approaches linear decay as the horizon grows. Empirically, our rotational interpretation and idealized spherical analysis provide useful predictions for LLM pretraining in practice, including schedule comparisons missed by existing analyses. Our analysis predicts schedule ordering across model scales for both vanilla (Adam, Muon) and Hyperball-style (AdamH, MuonH) optimizers. Our Hyperball experiments support the predicted strong performance of linear LR decay and confirm our prediction that WSD underperforms in this setting. Accounting for parameter norm dynamics, we predict instead the strong performance of WSD for Adam and Muon shown in practice. Guided by our theoretical insights, we also derive a new LR schedule for Adam and Muon, which improves over the established cosine and WSD schedules. All in all, these results support the use of rotational dynamics to understand, predict, and ultimately guide scheduling in LLM pretraining.

candidates.title: Single-Coordinate Activation Steering for Controllable Social Stance in Language Models
candidates.abstract: Steering one neuron of a small language model can impose a topic or a quirk without training, yet replications show that many published single-neuron recipes are fragile or nonspecific. This paper asks whether an interpersonal stance can be controlled in this manner. The stance studied is a distant crush, a chatbot character that is guarded, intermittently warm and inconsistent. In Qwen3.5, 4B, contrasting activations on hand-written guarded and eager replies identified neuron 7515 of layer 9 as a candidate for controlling this stance. Increasing this neuron activation made the characters replies more distant. Three language models rated this change as stronger than the effects of changing randomly selected neurons, and a blind human comparison supported the finding. Changing the interventions direction between messages also shifted replies between warmer and more distant styles. This suggests that a language model conversational stance can be personalized without finetuning.

candidates.title: LM2 Compiling a Language Model into Another Model Weights
candidates.abstract: Deploying a conversational model and a specialist together could avoid maintaining a separate specialist service. We present LM2, which embeds a trained story generator into a larger conversational model. The larger model handles the conversation and invokes the generator for story requests. We constrain the generator arithmetic during training so its calculations can be compiled directly into added model layers. We compare this approach with QwenPU, which executes the stories260K language model on an embedded processor. LM2 requires one host token per generated character, compared with approximately 25,000 for QwenPU. However, its story generator predicts held out text less well, i.e. 1.145 bits per character versus 0.894 for stories260K, where lower is better. The Qwen3.5, 0.8B implementation occupies 18.1 GB and generates the same characters as a standalone integer implementation of the inner model in the tested runs. These results illustrate a tradeoff between host-token cost and text-prediction performance.

candidates.title: Small-time global exact controllability of nonlinear Schrödinger equations on the circle with bilinear controls
candidates.abstract: We study nonlinear Schrödinger equations on the circle with nonlinearity $κ|ψ|^{2p}ψ$, a fixed smooth real potential $V$, and bilinear controls. Using only the three control potentials $\mathbf 1,\cos x,\sin x$, we prove global approximate controllability in $H^s$ on the unit sphere of $L^2$ for all integers $s,p\ge1$, every $κ\in\mathbb R$, and any prescribed positive time. The proof combines two ingredients: the approximate controllability between nowhere vanishing states from our companion paper, and a new mechanism that steers any nonzero initial state to a nowhere vanishing state in arbitrarily small time. When $V=0$ and the nonlinearity is defocusing or sufficiently weakly focusing, adding two explicit control potentials of finite regularity gives local exact controllability in $H^2$ near the constant state, via a moment problem and the inverse mapping theorem. Together, these results imply global exact controllability in $H^2$ on the unit sphere of $L^2$, at any prescribed positive time, with five control potentials. To~the best of our knowledge, this is the first global exact controllability result for a nonlinear Schrödinger equation with finitely many bilinear controls.

candidates.title: Non unitary and nonlinear quantum generative large model design and fast large-scale training without back propagation
candidates.abstract: Transformer-based large models require huge computational and storage costs. Quantum computation is expected to address that due to its potential to speed up classical algorithms exponentially. Key challenges of implementing quantum large models include the linear, unitary nature of qubit evolutions contrast with the non-unitary matrices and nonlinear functions in classical Transformers, as well as the difficulty of implementing gradient back-propagation on quantum hardware. Here we propose a fully quantum large model containing all the Transformer layers, implementing the non-unitary transformations through SVD-decomposition-based quantum circuits, and approximated nonlinear activation functions through pre-trained parameterized quantum circuits. We also propose a quantum circuit training algorithm based on multi-agent Reinforcement Learning, which can train large-scale parameterized quantum circuits without back-propagation. The dependency between the inference time complexity and the model's hidden dimension has been reduced from polynomial to logarithmic, showing an exponential advantage. The inference executions on the quantum hardware verify our model's 300-1000 times speed-up, and the measurements on the sequence-to-sequence tasks shows its learning ability. The training algorithm achieves only 25% complexity of the best SOTA quantum circuit training algorithms, especially this ratio decreases fast as the parameter scale increases. Our work not only proposes a quantum large model that can significantly reduce the computational cost, but also promotes the quantum computation towards general computing.

candidates.title: Bayesian Calibration of Computer Experiments and Extrapolation
candidates.abstract: Calibration, a fundamental inverse problem in uncertainty quantification, suffers from model identifiability issues. While the discrepancy decomposition model partially addresses this via a first-order Taylor expansion, it struggles when the approximation is biased. We propose a Bayesian modified discrepancy decomposition model that incorporates a residual process to capture higher-order discrepancy structures. By jointly inferring calibration parameters and model discrepancies within a Bayesian framework, our model recovers more physically meaningful parameters and provides reliable uncertainty quantification. Crucially, this accurate parameter recovery enables reliable extrapolative prediction, a challenge current methods largely fail to address. We validate the approach through numerical studies and a real-world industrial application: predicting the thermal stability of multilayer mirrors in extreme ultraviolet lithography. In this application, our method accurately predicts high-temperature responses far beyond the training domain, significantly outperforming existing calibration methods.

candidates.title: Think Before You Forecast: Scaling Test-Time Compute for Time Series Forecasting
candidates.abstract: Test-time compute has become an important paradigm in computer vision and language modeling, where additional computation at inference time enables models to explore multiple candidate solutions and select or refine the most reliable one. However, time series forecasting models typically produce predictions through a single forward pass, leaving them vulnerable to distribution shifts and non-stationarity that frequently arise in real-world temporal data. We propose Time Test Compute for Time Series (TTC4TS), an architecture-agnostic framework that improves the predictive performance of frozen forecasting models at inference time. Given a pretrained backbone, the generator produces multiple candidate forecast trajectories using augmentation, retrieval, adapter. The synthesizer then selects or combines these candidates using aggregation, classification, or candidate-scoring and ranking methods to produce the final forecast. By increasing the number of candidates, TTC4TS scales test-time compute without retraining the forecasting backbone. Beyond improving point-forecast accuracy, TTC4TS can exploit candidate forecasts for uncertainty quantification, which supports improved interval forecasts. We also theoretically analyze when additional test-time computation improves forecasting. Experiments across diverse datasets and backbones demonstrate consistent gains in accuracy and calibration. Code is provided in https://github.com/Anoise/TTC4TS.

candidates.title: Action Windows Are Inherently Temporal: A Benchmark for Time-Sensitive Robotic Manipulation
candidates.abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) agents have surpassed learned-policy baselines on existing robotic manipulation benchmarks. However, these agents still struggle with time-sensitive everyday tasks that existing benchmarks for VLM agents cover only partially. In these tasks, evolving physical processes create finite windows for successful intervention. These action windows are inherently temporal and impose a shared time budget on decision making and physical execution. Coordinating intervention within this budget requires agents to determine when the window opens. We introduce AWAIT, a simulation benchmark that evaluates task completion within action windows while accounting for decision and execution time.
