Under uniform transportation costs, the optimality conditions balance local and aggregate demand coverage and reduce to a scalar search under mild regularity conditions. We use this structure to develop an interpretable iterative heuristic for general metrics. The heuristic calibrates effective transportation costs from lateral shipments under independent stocking and uses them to construct location-dependent pooling weights. These weights have a direct operational interpretation through the cost of serving demand at other locations. Under the stated assumptions, the heuristic recovers the exact uniform-metric solution. Numerical experiments on structured and random networks show costs close to the sampled optimum on average and substantial savings relative to independent stocking.

candidates.title: DRAM: Memory-Efficient Muon via Rank Reallocation in Principal-Random Subspaces
candidates.abstract: Memory-efficient Muon methods aim to reduce storage overhead while preserving strong performance, yet existing approaches compromise either convergence guarantees or practical efficiency. In this paper, we focus on subspace optimization for Muon, where the choice of subspace determines the gradient information retained for updating. To preserve dominant information while providing the coverage needed for stochastic convergence guarantees, we construct a principal-random subspace that combines leading singular directions of the stochastic gradient with random directions sampled from their orthogonal complement. Under a fixed rank budget, there is a trade-off between principal exploitation and complementary coverage, making rank allocation important for practical optimization. Our key observation is that the preferred balance shifts from principal-heavy early in training to random-heavy later. Motivated by this shift, we propose \dram, a memory-efficient Muon optimizer that reallocates principal and random ranks across stages while maintaining momentum and performing matrix-sign normalization entirely in the subspace. Theoretically, we establish convergence guarantees for general rank-allocation schedules with nondecreasing coverage factors, obtaining rates of $O(T^{-1/4})$ in the stochastic setting and $O(T^{-1/2})$ in the deterministic setting, with fixed allocation as a special case. Using a simple linear reallocation schedule, \dram achieves the best low-memory performance across three pre-training scales and nine fine-tuning settings.

candidates.title: When Fog Becomes a Weapon: Atmospheric Attacks on Visible-Infrared Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Existing adversarial attacks on vision-language models (VLMs) and cross-spectral perception primarily rely on conspicuous, unnatural artifacts, such as vivid adversarial patches or active light beams, that lack physical stealthiness, whereas prior weather attacks largely overlook how one atmosphere simultaneously affects heterogeneous sensors. This raises a key scientific question: can a purely natural, shared fog environment simultaneously disrupt complementary visible and thermal infrared cues without artificial surface modifications? We introduce Fog Manipulation Attack (FMA), a zero-gradient attack that optimizes a common 3D fog state to induce simultaneous semantic failures in visible-infrared VLMs. FMA links shared, depth- and layer-aware atmospheric propagation along scene paths with band-specific imaging physics---visible airlight scattering and thermal path radiance---allowing one realistic fog state to erode both modalities' distinct cues. Experiments show that FMA more than doubles simultaneous failure rates over fidelity-matched random fog, transfers to captioning and VQA, and removes cross-modal compensation, where restoring a clean companion view recovers 64%--74% of lost dual-input VQA answers.
candidates.comment: 11 pages, 8 figures. Supplementary material (23 pages) is available as an ancillary file

candidates.title: CAR3T: Generalizable Calibration-Guided Reference-View Attention Reuse for Multi-View 3D Transformers
candidates.abstract: Feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction relies on global attention for cross-view aggregation, but the attention cost grows quadratically with the number of views, making inference increasingly expensive for larger inputs. Existing acceleration methods compress tokens or sparsify attention, potentially losing geometric detail or restricting cross-view aggregation while leaving redundancy among attention outputs underexploited. We observe similar cross-view attention distributions in certain layers, revealing an opportunity to reduce repeated global aggregation through output reuse. However, the layers suitable for reuse vary with the input, and reusing one layer alters the features received by later layers. Similarity at individual layers therefore cannot characterize the combined effect of multiple reuse decisions on output drift. To address these challenges, we propose CAR3T, a training-free framework combining reference-view attention output reuse with offline risk calibration and online dynamic layer selection. Calibration models cumulative reuse risk, while online selection adapts reuse to each input under a calibrated budget. CAR3T retains all input tokens and attends to the keys and values of all views, reducing the core attention computation in selected layers from quadratic to linear. Experiments on VGGT, DA3, and $π^3$ show forward speedups up to $1.41\times$ with at most 100 views and $1.75\times$ on longer sequences, with accuracy trade-offs across backbones and datasets.

candidates.title: CLOSE: A Calibrated Label-free Online Self-Evaluating Verifier for Object Hallucination in Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Vision-language models frequently describe objects absent from the image because of language priors. Yet the model itself is already a strong judge of its own output: asked separately whether an object is present, it rejects 44%-62% of its hallucinations, and its yes probability reaches an AUROC of 0.90-0.95 without training. This judgment, however, is not directly usable: (1) its probabilities lack a common scale across models; (2) for the remaining 38%-56%, the model still answers yes with probabilities that overlap those of real objects, so no threshold separates them. We therefore propose CLOSE, a Calibrated Label-free Online Self-Evaluating verifier that enforces this judgment during generation. Its threshold is a quantile of a memory rather than a probability and thus depends only on ranks; the memory is cold-started from unlabeled images and updated online. A scorer self-trained on pseudo-labels from four hidden-state signals is fused with self-asking by rank to separate what self-asking leaves mixed. Refused objects are rolled back and banned through a laddered back-off, and a recognition table intercepts their reappearance under other wordings. On COCO, refusing 20% and 40% of object mentions reduces the CHAIRs of LLaVA-1.5-7B by 42% and 87% (F1 +1.9 and -6.1 points); refusing 20% and 35% reduces the reachable hallucinations of Qwen3-VL-8B (official counts minus CHAIR-script miscounts) by 79% and 96% (F1 +0.5 and -5.3). An external vocabulary further extends the check beyond the official vocabulary.
candidates.comment: 41 pages (8-page main text and appendix), 25 figures, 24 tables

candidates.title: MedCoast: Semantic Abstraction of Reasoning Trajectories for Test-Time Biomedical Question Answering
candidates.abstract: Biomedical question answering often requires multi-step reasoning under limited inference budgets. While test-time search methods such as Tree-of-Thought can improve reasoning performance, directly searching over free-form language is computationally expensive and highly redundant, as many reasoning trajectories contain semantically equivalent intermediate steps expressed in different surface forms. We introduce MedCoast, an offline-to-online reasoning framework that converts sampled chain-of-thought trajectories into a compact space for structured process supervision. Offline, we recursively cluster semantically similar reasoning steps under shared prefixes to construct an abstract reasoning tree that captures recurring clinical reasoning patterns. We then derive node-level supervision from progress toward correct solutions, and train a lightweight process reward model (PRM) to evaluate partial reasoning states. At inference time, the learned critic guides test-time exploration by prioritizing promising reasoning prefixes. Across seven biomedical QA benchmarks, MedCoast often improves over self-consistency under fixed inference budgets, with gains of up to 15 points. Despite using a reward model more than 50 times smaller, MedCoast achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art reward models in several settings, highlighting its potential for resource-constrained biomedical reasoning.

candidates.title: AsyncMixVLA: Runtime Asynchronous Robot Policy Switching for Adaptation to Dynamic Environments
candidates.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models translate visual observations and language instructions into robot actions, enabling general-purpose robotic control. However, environmental perturbations, such as objects moving during execution, can undermine their reliability. Different policies exhibit complementary failures under mid-rollout perturbations, motivating selective switching between policies for recovery. Such switching can stall the robot during inference of the newly invoked policy or, if performed asynchronously, act on stale observations. We present AsyncMixVLA, an adaptive inference framework for proactive, asynchronous switching across heterogeneous VLA policies. A learned trigger balances recovery potential against intervention harm to selectively escalate to a higher-compute policy. AsyncMixVLA overlaps its inference with committed outgoing actions and aligns its context to the anticipated takeover state. On LIBERO-Long with mid-rollout perturbations, AsyncMixVLA improves perturbed task success from 69.5% to 77.1% over the lightweight policy. It achieves 84.9% overall success, comparable to 84.5% for synchronous switching, while reducing median exposed handoff latency from 226.5 ms to 0.1 ms. Without retraining or recalibration, it achieves 75.1% success across three unseen perturbation families, compared with 71.3% for the stronger constituent policy in aggregate.
candidates.comment: Manuscript prepared for the DAC 2027 Research Track (IEEE conference format)

candidates.title: Right Verdict, Right Reason? An Execution-Grounded Study of Whether LLM Vulnerability Detectors Understand Vulnerabilities
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to detect vulnerabilities, and their benchmark scores are often read as evidence that they understand the vulnerabilities they report. We test this reading against program execution. For 515 C and C++ functions from BigVul and PrimeVul whose vulnerability we reproduce with a proof of concept, we identify the line at which the fault occurs and the statements on which the faulting run depended. These facts ground a ladder of five tests, from telling a vulnerable function from its fixed version, through locating the fault and reacting to its removal, to judging execution-confirmed edits and predicting the outcome of a concrete run. Each test is paired with a baseline that needs no understanding, such as a rule that picks lines with risky calls, and we repeat the study on 195 vulnerabilities published after the training cutoffs of the models. Four findings emerge. First, telling a vulnerable function from its fixed version is hard. The open-weight models separate no more pairs than chance, although five of them show a weak sensitivity to the fix, and the commercial models still label many screened fixed versions vulnerable. Second, the commercial models locate the fault beyond a keyword rule, while removing that evidence changes the verdicts of the strongest model only on the newer vulnerabilities. Third, given the program input, the commercial models predict whether a run faults better than a rule that looks for added checks, and the prediction follows the input. Fourth, on the newer vulnerabilities this advantage disappears and the lead of the strongest model narrows, while localization persists. We release the framework, the per-function evidence, and an execution-confirmed counterfactual benchmark.

candidates.title: Tight Bounds for Rank Estimation in Turnstile Streams
candidates.abstract: We study rank estimation in turnstile streams. A frequency vector $f$ over the universe $[U]$ receives insertions and deletions. Given a query $x\in[U]$, the goal is to estimate the rank $\sum_{u<x}f_u$ within additive error $ε\|f\|_1$ with constant probability. The standard approach is Dyadic CountSketch by Luo, Wang, Yi and Cormode, using $\tilde{O}(ε^{-1}\log^{3/2}U\log n)$ bits, where $n$ is the final $\ell_1$ norm of $f$. Bulánek, Kumar, Meka, Nelson, and Sarlós placed this approach in a matrix-factorization framework. They improved the space of Dyadic CountSketch to $O(ε^{-1}\log^{3/2}U)$ words, and proved a lower bound of $Ω(ε^{-1}\log^2(εU))$ bits for all streaming algorithms when $U\le n\le U^{O(1)}$ and $ε=U^{-1+Ω(1)}$. This leaves a gap of $\sqrt{\log U}$. In this work, we fully determine the space cost of rank estimation up to an absolute constant. Our main result is a space lower bound for all streaming algorithms: for $0<ε\le 1/8$ and $n\ge\log^2 U$, the space is at least $Ω(\min\{ε^{-1}L^{3/2}\log(2+nε/\sqrt{L}), ε^{-2}\log U\log n, \log\binom{U+n}{n}\})$ bits, where $L=\log(2+Uε)$. When $U\le n\le U^{O(1)}$ and $ε=U^{-1+Ω(1)}$, this simplifies to $Ω(\min\{ε^{-1}\log^{5/2}U, ε^{-2}\log^2 U\})$ bits. Our proof uses a surprising hard distribution and novel information-theoretic techniques. The above bound matches Dyadic CountSketch when $n\ge U$ and $U^{-1+Ω(1)}\leε\le O(1/\sqrt{\log U})$. The lower bound is also tight in the remaining regimes. For $ε\ge(\log U)^{-1/2}$, there exists an algorithm that uses $O(ε^{-2}\log U\log n)$ bits using $\ell_1$ samplers. For $ε\le U^{-1+o(1)}$, we refine Dyadic CountSketch so that its space in bits matches the first term of the bound.
candidates.comment: 54 pages, 3 figures. The abstract is abridged to meet arXiv's length limit

candidates.title: Understanding and Mitigating the Fragility of Self-Rewarding Optimization
candidates.abstract: Self-rewarding optimization (SRO) promises to improve language models by enabling them to generate their own reward signals. Yet when and how SRO succeeds or fails remains poorly understood. We reveal that SRO is fundamentally fragile: even seemingly benign perturbations to training prompts can corrupt the self-generated preference signal and trigger iterative collapse. We demonstrate this through two prompt-level attacks that serve as controlled stress tests: a Re-Ranking attack that concentrates training on prompts where self-reward diverges from an oracle, and a Preamble attack that learns short prefixes inflating self-reward without any gain in oracle quality. To explain why these attacks succeed, we introduce self-reward fidelity (SRF), a metric quantifying on-policy agreement between self-evaluated and oracle rewards. We show that SRF can serve as a diagnostic signal of self-supervision reliability, and that controlled SRF perturbations induce a phase-transition region: SRO improves when SRF remains sufficiently high, but collapses once SRF drops below a model- and task-dependent threshold. This analysis motivates Projection Decoupling Defense, which suppresses SRO update components along directions to which the reward generator is locally sensitive, improving SRO robustness under adversarial conditions. This work sheds light on the fragility of SRO and charts promising directions toward making it more robust.

candidates.title: The Gerards-Schrijver conjecture on the Edmonds-Johnson property is false
candidates.abstract: An integral matrix $A$ has the Edmonds-Johnson property if, for all integral vectors $b,c,l,u$, the first Chvátal closure of $\{x: b\le Ax\le c,\ l\le x\le u\}$ equals its integer hull. Gerards and Schrijver conjectured that a totally half-modular matrix has the Edmonds-Johnson property if and only if it has no minor equal to one of two specific matrices, of size $3\times3$ and $3\times4$. We disprove this conjecture. We give a totally half-modular $5\times6$ matrix that does not have the Edmonds-Johnson property and has no minor equal to either matrix. It is a minimal obstruction: every proper minor has the Edmonds-Johnson property. The proofs work on a graph whose edges are the rows and bounds of the matrix, and on which the minor operations act by deleting, contracting and halving edges. For minimality, we reduce every proper minor to two classes of matrices known to have the Edmonds-Johnson property.

candidates.title: Tight Mistake-Abstention Tradeoffs for Sequential Prediction under Adversarial Injections
candidates.abstract: We study the sequential prediction problem introduced by Goel et al. (2023), where an adversary can inject arbitrarily many corrupted instances in an i.i.d. stream from a clean distribution $μ$, while the learner is allowed to abstain from making a prediction at no cost if the current instance was indeed injected. When $μ$ is unknown, Yu and Blanchard (2026) show a polynomial tradeoff between mistakes and false abstentions for classes with finite VC dimension and oblivious adversaries, but still leave open a significant gap between upper and lower bounds in their tradeoff landscape. In this paper, we propose the weighted shattering potential, and based on variants of this potential, provide gap-closing algorithms that essentially characterize the tradeoffs under various settings of interest: When $μ$ is known, our algorithm improves over Goel et al. (2023) and achieves their conjectured $O(d\log T)$ mistake bound; When $μ$ is unknown, for oblivious adversary, our guarantees are tight both in $T$ and in terms of the VC dimension $d$, which completely characterizes the abstention-mistake tradeoff in this setting and gives an $O(\sqrt{dT})$ balanced rate. For adaptive adversary, our results are tight up to $\operatorname{poly}(dD\log T)$ factors for structured classes with finite so-called reduction dimension $D$. Our guarantees also extend to censored feedback, where the label is hidden after an abstention.

candidates.title: An ADMM-Based Approach to the Large-Scale Geomagnetically Induced Current Blocker Placement Problem
candidates.abstract: We propose an Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM)-based approach for addressing the challenge of determining placements for geomagnetically induced current (GIC) blocking devices on large-scale transmission networks. Traditional formulations of this placement problem lead to mixed-integer nonlinear programs (MINLPs) that are difficult for state-of-the-art MINLP solvers, which often struggle to exploit problem structure and fail to produce high-quality solutions on large systems. To overcome these challenges, the proposed method employs a three-block ADMM decomposition enhanced with (i) partial linearization of the GIC-related nonlinearities, supported by conditions guaranteeing exactness, and (ii) heterogeneous penalty parameters that significantly accelerate convergence to high-quality local solutions. Numerical experiments on newly constructed large-scale benchmark systems (up to 10,000 buses) demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods by several orders of magnitude in runtime while producing solutions whose objective values closely approach the ideal all-blocker lower bound. These results highlight the effectiveness and scalability of the proposed approach for mitigation planning efforts in large transmission networks.

candidates.title: CLASP: Deciding Structure and Claims Before Decoding for Whole-Slide Pathology Report Generation
candidates.abstract: Whole-slide pathology report generation has advanced through stronger slide encoders, retrieved knowledge, and, recently, slide-level multimodal LLMs. However, these generators leave every report-level choice to the decoder: how long the report is, how it is organised, and which findings it states and where. On the standard PathText-BRCA benchmark, we find that these choices dominate n-gram overlap, as reports from the query's hospital selected without learning approach the state of the art, while decoders under-generate and fall back to the most frequent findings. We present CLASP, a decide-then-decode generator that makes these choices explicitly, once per slide. Before decoding, an Exemplar Structure Prior (ESP) takes the sentence plan and length from reports of image-similar cases, a Calibrated Claim Decision (CCD) selects the findings from calibrated slide posteriors, and a Claim-to-Sentence Placement (CSP) assigns each finding to a planned sentence. A Plan-Conditioned Decoder (PCD), refined by structure-anchored sequence training, then writes the report under these decisions. With 35M parameters, CLASP outperforms retrained report generators and slide-level LLMs of up to 7B parameters, matches the strongest published results, and generalises to lung cancer from unseen hospitals. Its decisions change what the reports state, not only their length, transfer to an LLM decoder, and can withhold what H&E cannot show: withholding receptor status leaves 23% fewer contradictions with clinical records than the same network without decisions.

candidates.title: LoopSight: Looped Vision Transformers with Gated Prediction Memory
candidates.abstract: Looped vision transformers extend computation for visual reasoning by repeatedly applying a shared Transformer core. A challenge is to preserve useful prediction information across loop iterations while allowing the computation state to evolve. In this paper we introduce LoopSight, a looped vision transformer that uses Gated Prediction Memory (GPM) to maintain a persistent prediction state for readout, separate from the core's evolving computation state. At each iteration, a cross-attention gate uses the core's candidate features, the previous prediction state, and the current task state to control writes at the patch and channel level. The model decodes its prediction from the updated memory. We condition the shared core on the current iteration using asymptotic loop encoding and train the model by supervising its prediction at loop counts sampled from a truncated Gaussian distribution. LoopSight outperforms LoopViT across three model scales on ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2. On ARC-AGI-1, LoopSight-Small achieves 67.4% pass@2, a gain of 6.6 percentage points over LoopViT-Small with comparable parameter counts and FLOPs. LoopSight also outperforms LoopViT on Visual Sudoku and ImageNet classification. Further analyses on ARC-AGI-1 show that LoopSight preserves more already-correct predictions and maintains more stable readout features as its computation state continues to evolve. The code will be released at https://github.com/feufhd/LoopSight.

candidates.title: EvoViM: Recursively Self-Evolving Visual Agents for Exploration with Deferred Queries
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents have shown promising capabilities in task-oriented environments. However, they still struggle when queries are deferred until after exploration, requiring them to retain visual evidence before knowing which details will matter. We introduce EvoViM, a recursively self-evolving framework in which a frozen multimodal model turns its own interaction experience into one visual program for memory and skills. The program retains images and computes directly on pixels, and its operations decide how this evidence is used in each task. During memory evolution, the same model traces failures in its visual trajectories to the operations that lost or misused evidence and revises them. It also rewrites the notes and analysis tools that guide later revisions, which then build on earlier findings and skip changes that have already failed. We evaluate EvoViM with three multimodal models on six tasks covering visual matching, spatial recall, and sequential decision-making, including three tasks with deferred queries. Across the six tasks, EvoViM improves the average score over AutoMem, the strongest baseline in the main comparison, by 31.3-47.6 points on held-out episodes. Programs written once from the initial environment instructions perform substantially worse, highlighting the value of interaction experience in shaping how visual evidence is retained and used. Code and dataset are available at https://evovim.github.io/.

candidates.title: MACE: Memory-Augmented Crop-Disease Evaluation of Frozen Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: In plant phenotyping, crop disease diagnosis has traditionally relied on expert assessment of visible symptoms and on models tailored to specific crops or diseases, and both are difficult to scale across field conditions. Recent methods provide frozen vision-language models with source-grounded knowledge bases that summarize the typical symptoms of each disease but describe little of how symptoms vary across individual cases. We introduce MACE (Memory-Augmented Crop-Disease Evaluation), a training-free method that supplements the knowledge base with a memory of symptom descriptions paired with known disease labels. MACE matches a description of the query image against this memory and retrieves only text descriptions and disease labels, so the query is the only image that the diagnosis model sees. Across ten crops, MACE with Claude Sonnet 5.5 improved accuracy over the knowledge-base baseline from 42.8% to 62.2% in distribution and from 50.7% to 57.0% on held-out image collections. Retrieved disease labels accounted for most of the gain, and adding the corresponding text descriptions improved in-distribution accuracy by about six percentage points.
candidates.comment: 7 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Project page: https://mace-bench.github.io/

candidates.title: Complex band-limited maximum likelihood: estimating the wave behind detected quanta
candidates.abstract: Detected photons and electrons land at positions drawn from $|ψ|^2$, yet it is $ψ$, phase included, that a wave equation propagates, and the state that produced the particles is often known only in part. A density estimator can recover $|ψ|^2$ directly from the positions, without any wave equation, but it discards the phase, and with it the state. We introduce complex band-limited maximum likelihood (complex BLML), which estimates $ψ$ itself by maximising the likelihood of the detected positions over exactly the intensities the physics allows: squared moduli of complex functions whose spectrum lies in a given set, such as a band, the shape of the aperture, or several modes for a partially coherent source. A single eigenvalue can certify a global maximum. On simulated two-slit far fields we measure what each prior is worth: a band reaches a given accuracy with seven times fewer photons than a kernel density estimate and already gives the fringe contrast and the relative phase, and the shape of the aperture adds the slit geometry. Some quantities need a prior at any number of photons: for slits of one profile the intensity fixes only the contrast $2ρV/(1+ρ^2)$, and on a line two different apertures can produce the same particles. Cutting a pattern to a few fringes, as published records are, removes the slit width. On four public single-particle double-slit records it predicts held-out particles best among the methods we tested, kernel estimators and two-slit optical models included, and it recovers the fringe contrast without a model of the optics. On fluorescent beads it finds the resolution limit of the microscope, $2\mathrm{NA}/λ$, from the photons alone.
candidates.comment: 13 pages, 6 figures; supplementary material as ancillary file. Submitted to Physical Review A

candidates.title: Making Repeated Variational Circuit Optimization Efficient on GPUs
candidates.abstract: Repeated numerical optimization is a defining workload for classical simulation of parameterized quantum circuits. Although successive training steps change gate parameters, they usually preserve circuit connectivity and reuse a small set of gate-layer patterns. We use this regularity to accelerate gradient evaluation on GPUs. Our framework combines execution primitives for common circuit layers with adjoint differentiation, coordinating state evolution and derivative computation to reduce launch overhead, intermediate storage, and state-vector traffic. Because effective schedules depend on circuit size, gate structure, and device resources, our framework retains several execution choices instead of committing to a single schedule. Structural and hardware constraints narrow these choices, after which measurements on representative layers guide plan selection. The selected plans are reused while circuit structure remains fixed, spreading the selection cost over repeated training iterations. This approach targets the computation required by optimization rather than forward simulation alone, while retaining the numerical semantics of state-vector differentiation. Experiments across multiple circuit families and GPU platforms compare our framework with the native GPU adjoint implementation in PennyLane Lightning. The results demonstrate substantially lower gradient evaluation times over the evaluated workloads, together with the numerical accuracy checks reported in the evaluation.

candidates.title: Jointly Recovering Destination Attractiveness and Spatial Preference Segments from Observed Tours via Inverse Optimization
candidates.abstract: Quantifying destination attractiveness by counting visitors, the most direct approach, can favor accessible sites and understate destinations that travelers reach at considerable cost. Preferences may also cut across a priori socio-demographic groupings. This study develops an inverse optimization framework that recovers destination attractiveness and preference segments jointly from observed multi-stop trip tours and generalized travel costs, without prespecifying tour-level segment assignments or imposing a parametric distribution on the unexplained part of utility. Representing each destination visit as a link in an extended network turns utility-maximizing tour choice into an inverse shortest paths problem. We apply the framework to 2,931 holiday vehicle trip tours over 51 target municipalities in Hokkaido, Japan. Constraint generation and alternating optimization make estimation tractable in this multi-destination setting, and the segments recovered under a three-segment specification show contrasting spatial preferences across the established coastal centers, the corridor around Sapporo, and the inland lake districts. The recovered values are expressed on a common monetary scale across destinations and segments without segment-specific scale normalization. They are uncorrelated with visit counts in the input data (r = -0.01) yet moderately correlated with tourist arrivals from an independent prefectural survey (r = 0.40), and are positively associated with the cost of reaching a destination (r = 0.60); destinations above this cost-value relationship include niche places that visit counts alone do not distinguish. The results provide a spatially explicit account of destination value and preference heterogeneity that can inform urban and regional planning and segment-targeted marketing.

candidates.title: When and Where to Transfer: Learning Transferable Historical Contexts for Short-History Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
candidates.abstract: Related sources can improve multivariate time series forecasting when the target history is short, but their usefulness varies across source groups and historical periods. A key challenge is to identify informative historical contexts from the sources. This paper proposes Hierarchical Context Transfer (HiCT), a framework that adaptively weights source groups and their historical contexts to determine both \emph{where} and \emph{when} to transfer. A shared context encoder and cross-attention are used to learn weights over source groups and historical contexts. These weights guide regularized transfer estimation, followed by an optional target-specific correction. This paper establishes a target excess-risk bound for the context-weighted transfer estimator. Experiments demonstrate competitive predictive performance across four multivariate forecasting datasets and a favorable accuracy--runtime trade-off against the evaluated baselines. Source-corruption ablations illustrate the roles of group-level and within-group weighting in adapting to unreliable source histories.

candidates.title: Modeling Perceived Promptness in Simultaneous Interpreting from Quality, Structure, and Timing Signals
candidates.abstract: Simultaneous interpreting requires interpreters to convey the source accurately while keeping pace with it in real time. Timing measures such as segment-onset delay capture part of this requirement, but may not fully reflect how professional evaluators judge promptness. We investigate whether these judgments can be explained by timing alone or whether the interpreted output provides additional information. Our dataset contains 622 Chinese-English and English-Chinese segments from 16 source speeches and seven interpreters. Two senior professional interpreters rated each segment for language quality (LQ), expressiveness (EXP), and perceived latency (LAT), which we also refer to as professional promptness. On held-out source speeches, onset delay alone achieves a Pearson correlation of r = .318 with LAT ratings. Combining predicted LQ and EXP with delay improves the correlation to r = .475. Lexical and structural features provide a stronger signal, reaching r = .632 when combined with delay and r = .658 when predicted quality is also included. These results suggest that professional promptness judgments reflect properties of the interpreted output beyond when the interpreter begins speaking. The additional contribution of predicted quality over structural features, however, is modest. Although the two evaluators differ in how strongly quality relates to LAT, cross-evaluator predictions remain positively correlated with LAT ratings. The overall pattern also holds when each interpreter is held out in turn.

candidates.title: Beyond Unit Tests: Path-Aware Rubric-Guided LLM Autograding of Notebooks
candidates.abstract: Jupyter notebooks support open-ended, multi-step assessments in which students build one logical flow across interdependent steps, combining code, written analysis, and generated outputs such as plots. These reflect authentic scientific practice but are hard to grade consistently, since students may make different yet equally valid choices at each step, so a later answer can only be judged in light of the choices a student made earlier. We present an LLM-based autograder for such flow-structured notebook questions. It generates a rubric from a reference solution, then applies a softening pass that relaxes criteria tied to the reference so legitimate alternative paths are not penalized. Each question group is graded in a single model call, so later answers are judged against the student's own earlier choices, using question-type tags and schema-constrained, low-temperature outputs. Evidence is scored multimodally: code, text, numerical outputs, and figures from code cells. We deployed the tool in a machine-learning course, integrated with Gradescope, with a pre-submission format check and prompt-injection defenses, and evaluate it both in that live course and against archived submissions graded by staff in earlier terms. We report agreement, cross-model variance, cost, student perceptions, and injection resilience. With low-temperature models, agreement with human scores is often strong, including on the open-ended items the design specifically targets, while run-to-run stability depends sharply on the model's temperature support.

candidates.title: Tool-to-Self: Internalizing Visual Tool Capabilities via Scaffolded Reinforcement Learning
candidates.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly rely on external visual tools to access fine-grained visual evidence, but repeated tool execution incurs substantial inference overhead and deployment dependencies. Moreover, conventional tool-use RL can improve visual-task performance, yet the resulting tool gains are often unstable. Motivated by this, we propose Tool-to-Self (T2S), a tool-scaffolded reinforcement learning framework that turns external visual tools into temporary training scaffolds. T2S cold-starts tool-use ability and observation prediction from tool-repairable examples, then progressively anneals tool execution on a per-tool basis during RL. By combining answer-correctness and observation-consistency rewards with privileged on-policy self-distillation from actual tool observations, T2S effectively teaches the model both to reproduce tool outputs and to reason from them. Experiments across diverse visual perception and reasoning benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over both explicit tool-use models and implicit zooming models while enabling tool-free inference with reduced latency.

candidates.title: Selective ROM Weight Storage for Responsive LLM Control on Edge Robots
candidates.abstract: Edge robots increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for complex tasks, demanding efficient inference alongside timely control. Limited memory capacity constrains model deployment, while repeated weight transfers during decoding compete with activations and KV cache for external bandwidth. Sequential generation of robot actions further delays decisions and periodic control on shared hardware. We present a hybrid memory architecture with heterogeneous scheduling to address these bottlenecks jointly. Banked ROM stores selected fixed weights and supplies a standard compute array through a dedicated datapath. LPDDR retains the remaining weights and mutable state, preserving model flexibility. Coordinated operand delivery and preemption at output slice boundaries accelerate inference while limiting interference with periodic control. A structured decision interface scores candidate phases in a single forward pass, avoiding sequential token generation for routine choices. Together, these mechanisms improve memory service, compute access, and decision execution for edge robotic workloads. Experiments with Qwen3-8B achieve a peak decode speedup of 1.56$\times$ and reduce P99 task response time by a factor of approximately 227.27$\times$, while completing 100.00\% of the tested grasping and transport tasks.

candidates.title: SAFE-DRIFT: Data Selection for Supervised Fine-tuning with Controllable Off-Target Drifts
candidates.abstract: We propose SAFE-DRIFT, a data-selection framework for supervised fine-tuning that improves a target capability while controlling unwanted drift in the model's other behaviors. We formalize this as a constrained optimization problem that maximizes alignment with the target gradient, subject to a budget on off-target drift which we quantify using the Fisher information of a reference distribution. Under this objective, the optimal, closed-form update is a damped natural-gradient step that downweights reference-sensitive directions. To estimate these high-dimensional gradients and work within the right geometry, we further derive a scalable algorithm that approximates the Fisher information and the target gradient in a shared low-dimensional subspace and analyze how entanglement of the target and reference task can affect the update. We evaluate SAFE-DRIFT against state-of-the-art data selection methods across diverse domains including coding and medical question answering, yielding competitive target performance while reducing degradation on specified off-target behaviors.

candidates.title: From atomic events to material degradation across metre and year scales
candidates.abstract: Material degradation emerges from microscopic events whose consequences accumulate over years, yet mechanism-resolved simulations remain confined below engineering timescales. The challenge is not just the sheer number of events: atomistic evolution is dominated by recurrent local motion, with only a tiny fraction driving lasting structural change. This distinction is not encoded in an instantaneous atomic configuration. Locally indistinguishable states can exhibit different event competition, escape times, and long-horizon outcomes, revealing missing kinetic context as a critical information bottleneck. This context spans space and time: the future consequence of a local transition depends on its surrounding defect environment and the kinetic history leading to its current state. To solve this, AtomWorld reconstructs a predictive kinetic state from multiscale structural observations and trajectory history, distinguishing transient fluctuations from microscopic pathways that drive persistent structural evolution. Learning operates only over transitions admitted by the underlying kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) process, preserving event legality, state evolution, and physical time. Across BCC Fe-Cu precipitation, FCC Ni-Cr-Al ordering, and HCP Zr-H interstitial transport, restoring kinetic context consistently advances persistent evolution while maintaining physical fidelity and transferring to unseen conditions. In irradiated reactor-pressure-vessel steel, this approach achieves up to 420-fold greater persistent evolution under matched event budgets. Combined with scalable execution, it successfully extends mechanism-resolved trajectories to service-year timescales across metre-scale heterogeneous domains.

candidates.title: From Reward Engineering to Data-Centric Reinforcement Learning for Effective Agentic Visual Tool Use
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly use external visual tools to acquire evidence during reasoning, yet learning when to invoke these tools remains challenging. Existing tool-use reinforcement learning (RL) methods often rely on call-contingent rewards to encourage beneficial tool use, but such reward engineering can distort the task objective and lead to degenerate calling behaviors. We argue that effective tool-use learning requires identifying not merely which questions are difficult, but which failures are attributable to missing visual evidence and can therefore be corrected through tool observations. We propose AOVO, a data-centric framework that enables MLLMs to learn effective tool use through perception attribution and policy-adaptive data sampling (PADS), without introducing tool-specific rewards. It counterfactually probes the model's reasoning states to identify observation-sensitive questions, distinguishing them from reasoning-dominated ones. PADS then periodically estimates category-level observation effects from recent policy rollouts and dynamically reallocates the training distribution toward questions where visual observations provide informative learning signals, while optimizing solely for final-answer correctness. Experiments across diverse visual perception and multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over competitive tool-use MLLMs, with causal analysis further validating the data-centric perspective for learning effective visual tool use.

candidates.title: Data-driven discovery of sparse governing equations with parameterized operators
candidates.abstract: We study parameterized SINDy (pSINDy), an extension of the Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) framework for the discovery of parsimonious governing equations involving operators with unknown parameters such as fractional-order Caputo derivatives, fractional Laplacians, and parameterized kernel operators. The framework jointly identifies the unknown operator parameters and sparse library coefficients through a sparsity-promoting optimization problem. To solve this problem, we develop and analyze the parameterized sequentially thresholded least-squares (pSTLSQ) algorithm. In each iteration, it removes terms with small coefficients, updates the operator parameters by a fixed number of optimization steps that improve the fit of the remaining library terms, and refits their coefficients by least squares. Under suitable assumptions, we prove that pSTLSQ converges locally to a local minimizer and give sufficient conditions for identifying the terms present in the governing equation. Numerical experiments demonstrate recovery of governing equations from noisy synthetic data for fractional ODEs, fractional PDEs, and nonlocal diffusion equations. We also examine the influence of the hyperparameters, discretization scheme, and noise, and compare pSTLSQ with two benchmark methods. All three methods identify the correct terms at low noise levels, but differ in parameter accuracy, cost, and sensitivity to initialization and the candidate library.

candidates.title: The abc index: Exact Retrieval for Learned Sparse Representations
candidates.abstract: In learned sparse retrieval (LSR), queries have tens of terms with learned weights, on which classic dynamic pruning is believed to fail, and approximate indexes such as Seismic and HNSW are considered faster than exact ones. We challenge this view with abc, an exact index built only from standard IR techniques: term-at-a-time (TAAT) evaluation, Block-Max MaxScore, binary packing and doc-id reordering. They are combined in a new design and engineered for modern CPUs. On MS MARCO encoded with four LSR models, the abc index is the fastest exact index at every k: 6.5-84x faster than the exact search of Qdrant, 13-55x faster than that of Lucene, and 2.9-18x faster than BMP with an index 5-7x smaller. Against approximate indexes, it takes 1.5-3.6x less space, and its latency grows much more slowly with k: they are up to 4.3x faster at k=10, but at k=1000 it overtakes them, by up to 7.4x. Exactness comes with an extra benefit: there are no parameters to tune.

candidates.title: WorldWeave: Rethinking Embodied Navigation through Cross-Task World Modeling
candidates.abstract: Mobile embodied agents continuously alter their observations through their own motion, while external dynamics further shape future interactions. Different mobile embodied tasks therefore capture complementary patterns of state evolution, yet jointly learning world dynamics across such interactions remains less explored. We investigate this problem through Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) and Embodied Visual Tracking (EVT), which respectively involve navigation toward a stationary goal and interaction with a moving target. We propose WorldWeave, a cross-task world model that couples shared predictive dynamics with task-specific adaptation. Instead of conditioning state transitions on heterogeneous physical actions, WorldWeave learns latent actions from observed state changes via inverse-forward dynamics, establishing a shared transition representation across tasks. The resulting future-state predictions are adaptively integrated into task-specific representations for downstream decision making. Experiments across multiple VLN and EVT benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over specialized baselines.

candidates.title: Praxis: Practical Witness Encryption for NP
candidates.abstract: Witness encryption encrypts a message to an NP statement so that whoever holds a witness can decrypt. Over a decade after its introduction, known constructions for general NP statements are far from practical or rest on heuristic or broken assumptions. We propose Praxis, a practical scheme for NP, and prove it extractable in the bilinear generic group and random oracle models under Module-SIS. Our instantiation encrypts to a Groth16 verifier on BN254, set up honestly, which serves every NP relation at the same cost: at $100$-bit security, its ciphertext is $7.88$ GiB, encryption takes $2^{34.2}$ base-field multiplications, and decryption with a Groth16 proof $2^{33.0}$ on average. We give Lean 4 proofs of correctness and extraction at this instantiation's parameters. Praxis starts from the rank-gap template of the recent feasibility result [Hair and Sahai, arXiv 2026]. Where they raise the gap to keep decryption polynomial, we fix it, so decryption ends with a search that is exponential but concretely fast: $O(2^{λ/4} N^{1/4})$ expected operations for a statement in $N$ Boolean unknowns at $λ$-bit security. A quadratic arithmetic program makes our hidden matrix low rank, so where their ciphertext encodes a basis of a matrix space, ours holds factors of width two, which a pairing multiplies. Weights and identities from an extension field tie copies of this matrix, so an adversary telling encryptions apart yields a witness or a Module-SIS solution. For the same Groth16 statement and $100$-bit security level, Praxis reduces the ciphertext size and the cost of encryption of either of their constructions by over ten orders of magnitude, and that of decryption by over six.

candidates.title: PhysPPF: Learning Robotic Manipulation with Past, Present, and Future Physical Representations
candidates.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have advanced robotic manipulation, yet complex tasks requiring both precise 3D contact and long-horizon coordination remain challenging. Most existing studies enhance spatial perception or temporal reasoning in VLAs separately. Spatial methods primarily inject geometric or affordance priors into current-frame perception without tracking multi-step transitions, while history-aware and world-model VLAs typically capture past context or future dynamics in 2D feature or pixel spaces, either lacking explicit 3D contact cues or incurring high generation overhead. To address this, we propose PhysPPF, a VLA framework that performs unified spatiotemporal modeling in a compact physical token space. Spatially, WWH (What-Where-How) distills pretrained perception teachers exclusively during training into compact token groups capturing what 3D structures occupy the scene, where to interact, and how the gripper should approach, without test-time 3D encoders. Temporally, operating directly in this WWH space without pixel reconstruction, PPF (Past-Present-Future) consolidates executed states into a bounded past physical memory and jointly infers present and future physical tokens via an asymmetric world model. Parallel gated branches then inject these past, present, and future representations into a flow-matching action expert to guide manipulation without cross-temporal interference. Extensive experiments on SimplerEnv, CALVIN, and LIBERO show that PhysPPF consistently outperforms existing spatial, history-aware, and world-model VLAs with modest latency and parameter overhead, improving over the StarVLA baseline by +17.2 points on SimplerEnv, +29.3 points on CALVIN, and +3.5 points on LIBERO.

candidates.title: CCAMoE: Cache-Conditioned Adaptive Inference for Offloaded MoE
candidates.abstract: Expert offloading enables Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference on memory-constrained GPUs, but expert transfers and CPU execution limit decoding performance. Speculative decoding can mitigate these costs, yet separate draft weights consume scarce GPU memory and longer drafts increase verification demand. In this paper, we present CCAMoE, a unified runtime that coordinates adaptive speculative decoding with concurrent expert-cache updates. Its design has three key features: 1) Cache-only drafting, which reuses resident target experts to generate proposals and routing hints without separate draft weights; 2) Draft-guided cache updates, which anticipate expert demand and overlap transfers with computation to support subsequent drafting and verification; and 3) Cost-aware draft-length control, which balances expected acceptance against execution cost. Together, these mechanisms coordinate proposal generation and cache preparation through a shared evolving cache, improving proposal quality while reducing verification cost. Across various MoE models, GPU platforms, and workloads, CCAMoE consistently achieves the lowest decoding latency, with up to 2.33$\times$ speedup over state-of-the-art baselines.

candidates.title: Analyzing Atypical Local Features in Museum Artifacts using Generative Image Inpainting
candidates.abstract: This study proposes a method for analyzing local visual features in museum artifacts that may appear atypical or unexpected. Objects in the same category often share a similar overall shape, while local details such as patterns, decorations, and facial expressions may reflect regional or cultural characteristics. We use the appearance distribution learned by an image generation model as a reference for what is generally expected within an artifact category. For each target region, we exclude images from that region and fine-tune a generative model using only images from the remaining regions. We then mask selected parts of artifact images from the target region and ask the region-excluded model to complete them. If the completed result differs greatly from the original image, the masked part may contain features that are difficult to predict from the appearance learned from other regions. We measure this difference using LPIPS and treat it as reconstruction difficulty for the generative model. We conduct experiments on images of kokeshi dolls, drums, and masks from the collection of the National Museum of Ethnology. For each category, we select several target regions, build region-excluded LoRA models, and perform inpainting on predefined local parts. The results show that typical shapes and simple decorations are often reconstructed consistently, whereas some region-specific colors, patterns, cord arrangements, and painted details are replaced with more common appearances. These results suggest that region-excluded inpainting can serve as an exploratory tool for finding region-specific local visual features in museum artifact images.

candidates.title: X-AQA: Unifying Action Quality Assessment with Multimodal Large Language Models and Multi-Domain Learning
candidates.abstract: Action Quality Assessment (AQA) aims to evaluate the quality of human actions, yet existing methods are predominantly developed and evaluated on individual datasets with different task formulations and assessment criteria. We introduce X-AQA, the first unified training and evaluation framework for general-purpose AQA with multimodal large language models (MLLMs). We construct X-AQA-40K, a training corpus comprising 40,163 samples from 22 data sources across four domains: competitive sports, fitness exercises, rehabilitation, and general skills. We convert heterogeneous annotations into a unified question-answering format, incorporating dataset-specific annotation guidelines and official scoring rules when available. Using this corpus, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B to develop a single MLLM capable of handling diverse AQA tasks. We further establish X-AQA-Bench, which evaluates both in-distribution (ID) performance on datasets represented during training and out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization on four held-out datasets. The resulting model outperforms all evaluated open-source MLLMs on X-AQA-Bench and achieves competitive performance relative to proprietary MLLMs. Ablation studies further demonstrate that multi-domain joint training and explicitly providing assessment criteria in prompts both improve OOD generalization. X-AQA establishes a unified foundation for advancing general-purpose AQA across diverse real-world domains. Data and models are released at \hyperlink{https://huggingface.co/collections/Kelly0510/x-aqa}{here}.

candidates.title: SBTenv: A Literature-Validated Split-Belt Treadmill Simulation Environment
candidates.abstract: The split-belt treadmill is an important tool for studying human locomotor adaptation. Physics-based simulations complement such experiments by allowing hypotheses about the mechanisms of adaptation to be tested directly, and high-throughput simulation is increasingly needed as these models grow in complexity. However, no open-source split-belt treadmill environment exists in MuJoCo, a physics engine widely used for high-throughput simulation. Here, we present SBTenv, a split-belt treadmill environment built in MuJoCo and validated against published experimental data from a rimless wheel walking passively on a split-belt treadmill. By modeling compliant contacts at the spoke tips, SBTenv reproduces the experimental average steady velocity ($R^2=0.643$, RMSE $=0.0162$ m/s) without the empirical geometric correction required in prior simulations. We expect SBTenv, openly shared, to enable high-throughput simulation of musculoskeletal and robotic locomotion on a split-belt treadmill.
candidates.comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Code available at https://github.com/PhilipByrn3/sbtenv

candidates.title: Reconstruction-Guided Dual-Branch Learning for LiDAR Anomalous Object Detection
candidates.abstract: Detecting unexpected objects is essential for autonomous driving safety. Most existing LiDAR anomaly detectors rely on semantic discrimination, which primarily captures category-discriminative features but may overlook deviations from broader feature relationships in normal scenes. Reconstruction offers a complementary perspective by assessing consistency with learned normal patterns. However, pointwise reconstruction errors alone struggle to distinguish anomalies from normal variability in complex outdoor point clouds. We propose Structured Residual Reasoning (SRR) to extract additional anomaly evidence from residual structure across feature channels, time sequences, and geometric space. We further establish that semantic discrimination and normal-pattern reconstruction capture fundamentally different yet complementary anomaly evidence: category compatibility and consistency with learned normal patterns, respectively. At matched background false-positive rates, SRR recovers more objects missed entirely by the semantic branch while producing fewer false positives in normal-only scenes. Building on this finding, we propose Reconstruction-Guided Dual-Branch (RGDB) learning, in which SRR-derived normal-pattern consistency cues guide a semantic-conditioned anomaly decoder to complement reconstruction-based predictions during training. At inference, the two branches jointly exploit their complementary anomaly evidence. Experiments show that standalone SRR establishes a strong reconstruction-based baseline without semantic labels from the target-scene training data, while RGDB achieves state-of-the-art performance on the STU validation set.

candidates.title: Centerline-Guided Multi-Class Road Surface Segmentation
candidates.abstract: Road-surface extraction from satellite imagery supports geo- graphic mapping, but a binary mask leaves road axes, transverse extent, and junction structure implicit. Learning these proper- ties together is challenging because narrow corridors, merging roads, and occlusions require different geometric cues. We present a centerline-guided multi-class segmentation framework that makes these dependencies explicit. A hierarchical encoder sup- plies shared features, while predicted centerline features and soft probabilities condition specialized regular, intersection, and over- pass decoders. A two-component width branch supplies transverse geometry to regular-surface decoding, and learned feature fusion produces the complete road mask. Unlike independent prediction heads or a fixed union of component masks, this design exchanges geometric information during decoding while retaining separately inspectable outputs. Evaluation of the four-semantic-output con- figuration on CHN6-CUG achieves 65.53% complete-surface IoU, improving on a binary SegFormer-B4 baseline by 1.01 percentage points and reducing false-positive pixels by 11.94%. The results support geometry-aware surface refinement and a richer raster representation for road-map inspection.

candidates.title: Weight-Space Backdoors in Open-Weight LLMs: Cross-Architecture Attacks and Blind Model Forensics
candidates.abstract: Open-weight language models are vulnerable to trigger-conditioned behaviors introduced through sparse post-training weight modifications, creating supply-chain risks beyond conventional provenance checks. We present Neural Sentinel, a cross-architecture study of gradient-guided backdoor insertion and model forensics spanning 18 checkpoints across 14 architecture families (124M-31.3B parameters), including state-space and recurrent models. On Phi-2, modifying approximately 0.0002% of parameters induced an exact short-marker output after 300 steps (332 seconds), with mean next-token KL divergence of $1.5 \times 10^{-5}$ and 100% top-1 agreement over evaluated positions of eight fixed reference prompts. Separate experiments produced structured tool-call-formatted outputs without establishing downstream execution. We identify three procedure-dependent response regimes -- Gradient-Permeable, Scale-Threshold, and Gradient-Fragmented -- and evaluate PPO-based weight-space exploration, which showed no statistically significant advantage over random search. For defense, Neural Sentinel combines weight-difference analysis, trigger discovery, activation probing, and contextual output inspection. In a 22-artifact development cohort, its reference-optional scanner classified 4/5 backdoored artifacts as BACKDOORED; the remaining positive and all 17 clean artifacts were SUSPICIOUS. These findings establish the feasibility of sparse conditional-output insertion and evidence-producing forensic triage, while identifying limitations in behavioral-drift assessment and clean-model admission.

candidates.title: BIRD-Persona: A Persona-Aware Benchmark for SQL and pandas Analytics Code Generation
candidates.abstract: Production text-to-code systems use large language models to turn natural-language analytics requests into executable SQL and pandas code. Existing benchmarks cover both tasks but do not isolate when performance diverges between them. We introduce BIRD-Persona, a persona-stratified extension of BIRD-Python that adds novice and expert rewrites to tasks with matched SQL and pandas ground truth, along with schema variants and task-structure annotations. Across 1,534 tasks, nine models, and 245,592 evaluations, SQL outperforms pandas for eight of nine systems. The gap varies by condition: expert, schema-explicit prompts improve both paradigms but help SQL more; schema representations have mixed, model-dependent effects; and selected-column burden widens the gap while subqueries do not. By making user phrasing a controlled benchmark dimension, BIRD-Persona supports persona-aware and paradigm-aware evaluation of natural-language analytics systems. The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/optum-cognition-lab/BIRD-Persona.
candidates.journal_ref: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing: Industry Track, pp. 2311-2332 (2026)

candidates.title: A $(3/2+\varepsilon)$-Approximation for Weighted 3-Set Packing
candidates.abstract: We give a deterministic $(3/2+\varepsilon)$-approximation for weighted $3$-set packing, for every fixed rational $\varepsilon>0$, improving on the 1.6908-approximation reported by Tong and Xu (2026). The algorithm has two phases. It first performs bounded local search using a rounded $12/7$-power potential. It then combines compatible exchanges that insert at most three sets and increase the original weight. The analysis relates the gap left by the first phase to the gain available to the second phase. We prove a structural inequality that bounds the weight of a comparison packing by $3/2$ times the current weight plus one sixth of a sum of small-exchange gains. Each gain accounts for all sets that the exchange must delete. A greedy rule recovers enough of these gains to obtain the approximation guarantee. We derive the structural bound from local optimality by analyzing finite computation trees and averaging the error caused by their limited depth. The running time is $n^{4^{O(1/\varepsilon)}}\operatorname{poly}(L)$, where $n$ is the number of input sets and $L$ is the input encoding length. The same guarantee holds for maximum-weight independent set in induced $K_{1,4}$-free graphs.

candidates.title: Hierarchical Sub-Array Beam Training for Flexible Intelligent Metasurface-Enabled Hybrid Near-Far-Field Multiuser Communications
candidates.abstract: Low-resolution discrete phase shifters (PSs) are attractive for extremely large-scale arrays, but phase quantization distorts near-field (NF) beam patterns and degrades beam training and multiuser transmission. Moreover, the distinct codebook structures required by NF and far-field (FF) users complicate hybrid NF-FF beam training and codeword switching. To address these challenges, we introduce flexible intelligent metasurface (FIM) surface shaping as an additional geometric beamforming degree of freedom. We establish the hybrid NF-FF channel and beam pattern models, characterize the grating lobes induced by discrete PSs, and develop a phase-quantization compensation method. A deformation-range analysis shows that wavelength-scale shaping can achieve beam patterns comparable to those obtained with continuous PSs. We further propose a hierarchical sub-array beam training (HSABT) scheme that progressively doubles the activated central aperture according to the beam-width and beam-depth characteristics. A beam-intersection-based sampling strategy improves the angle-distance resolution, while a measurement-driven adaptive NF-FF beam-switching mechanism selects the final codeword without relying on the Rayleigh distance or prior user-location information. HSABT is also extended to multi-path channels through adaptive peak detection and inter-level energy-consistency-based candidate tracking. For high-gain multiuser transmission, we develop an alternating-optimization-based design and a complementary non-iterative key observation method, and analyze their convergence, computational complexity, and steady-point properties.Simulation results demonstrate continuous-phase-comparable beam patterns, reduced training overhead, more accurate main-path acquisition than exhaustive polar-codebook training, and higher multiuser sum rates than conventional rigid-array benchmarks.
candidates.journal_ref: IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Communications, 2026

candidates.title: LEAF: Calibrated and Robust Wavelet Estimation of the Hurst Exponent
candidates.abstract: Wavelet logscale regression for the Hurst exponent H of fractional Brownian motion (fBm) is sensitive to outliers and biased in finite samples. We introduce the Log-Energy with Adaptive Floor (LEAF) ordinate, which averages the logarithms of squared wavelet coefficients after adding a floor proportional to a pilot estimate of the level variance. If standardized coefficients share a common law across levels, a floor proportional to the true level variance preserves the population slope, and a consistent pilot preserves it asymptotically. We derive the asymptotic variance and influence function, and identify the variance-minimizing floor for median-pilot LEAF, whose influence grows only logarithmically. With outliers of ten increment standard deviations in up to 1% of observations, median-pilot LEAF reduces root mean squared error by a factor of 1.8 to 2.6 relative to calibrated log-energy. At H = 0.5 with 1% outliers, the error falls from 0.139 to 0.059. For small to moderate H, the main source of bias is the departure of expected wavelet energies from the ideal power law at fine scales. We estimate H from an estimating equation calibrated by simulation under fBm. Calibrating the mean logscale diagram alone delivers nearly all of the gain: it nearly eliminates bias in matched simulations and improves on the Abry--Veitch estimator most at small H. Simulations also show how scale-dependent tails can erode the gains of a robust pilot and how misspecification can undermine calibration.

candidates.title: Where the Image Sits: Vision-Text Order Bias in Jev
candidates.abstract: Jev-style system-1 decision models read a choice from a single prefill. They restrict the next-token distribution to the supplied option labels and return a distribution over the options, with no generation and no parsing. Recent work shows that generative vision-language models are sensitive to the relative order of image and text tokens. We ask whether that sensitivity reaches this Jev-style readout. The answer is always read at the end of the prompt, so moving the image changes the distance from the visual evidence to the decision, but never the position at which the decision is read. Using four placements---prefix, pre-question, pre-options, and suffix---and holding the option listing fixed, we measure argmax flips, total variation, accuracy, calibration, and label marginals. Suffix placement flips 41.0% of decisions and lowers accuracy by 18.6 points. Averaged over the four slots, the curve is monotone, not U-shaped. That shape differs from prior results on generative vision-language models. The effect survives a battery of controls. We also introduce prefix--question averaging (P+Q), a two-forward readout that averages the prefix and pre-question distributions. It is at least as accurate as prefix and outperforms the prior baselines. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/Youzhi333/Visual_Tex_Order_Bias_Jev.

candidates.title: Walks2Maps: Learning Indoor Geometry from Crowdsourced Wi-Fi RTT and Motion Trajectories
candidates.abstract: Everyday smartphone walks offer a scalable source of indoor geometry, but their motion traces drift and their radio measurements are distorted by multipath. We present Walks2Maps, a physics-guided framework that reconstructs a shared metric map from Wi-Fi round-trip-time (RTT) and motion observations, without a floor plan, surveyed access-point (AP) coordinates, or position labels. Walks2Maps jointly estimates pedestrian trajectories, AP locations, and per-trajectory stride scales, then recovers the pathway layout from the reconstructed paths. Shared AP observations connect walks recorded in different local frames, while metric ranges constrain their relative geometry and scale. An asymmetric range loss accommodates multipath-induced excess delay. On 22 phone trajectories collected along 11 routes on an office floor with 30 APs, Walks2Maps achieves median AP and trajectory errors of 0.87 m and 0.89 m, respectively, and a walked-area F1 score of 0.985. Ablations show that radio similarity can recognize places while still producing a distorted map; retaining the metric information in RTT resolves this ambiguity. Asymmetric modeling further reduces AP error by 54% relative to a symmetric loss. These results demonstrate how radio and motion measurements can jointly reveal indoor geometry without a dedicated mapping survey. We will release the dataset and toolkit.
candidates.comment: This paper is accepted to NeurIPS 2026 PhysWorldAI Workshop

candidates.title: Mechanism Design under Belief Disagreement: Allocation Flexibility and Rent Capacity
candidates.abstract: A seller jointly chooses allocation and payments when buyers misperceive competition. Under independent private values, statewise participation, and payment restrictions, allocation determines both required rents and their delivery capacity. We separate these effects under a common subjective law. For three values and shared-top beliefs, explicit score and capacity conditions characterize globally optimal lower-value lotteries, including top-rent overflow and welfare differences among revenue optima. A two-buyer construction establishes a strict allocation advantage over every reserve under the same fixed reporting certificate and positive margin. A transport test and exact band-boundary incentive equalities identify separate conditions restoring objective-law revenue ceilings. For three bands and a common affine belief interval, an explicitly certified reserve attains the ceiling under stated score conditions. A case scaled to public collectible-auction records yields a nominal shared-top allocation gain of 24.72 cents per auction. A one-cent report-by-report margin yields matched gains of 1.48 cents under projection and 3.32 cents under shared-top beliefs; the three-band point-belief gain of 2.50 cents disappears with common-interval protection. These comparisons bound the additional recurring costs an allocation redesign can cover at the specified reporting requirement.

candidates.title: General-purpose language models are neurosymbolic reasoners able to annotate proteins from sequence
candidates.abstract: Determining the function of genes across the tree of life is one of the major challenges in biology. Generative AI approaches to this problem generally fall into two categories: language models trained on biological sequences that are able to predict structure and function from signals in those sequences; and generalist language models trained on text, that are able to reason about biological function symbolically. A default operating assumption is that protein language models do not perform well on symbolic tasks, and that generalist language models do not perform well on sequence tasks. However, a recent report showed that frontier generalist models perform surprisingly well on next-residue prediction tasks. We set out to explore whether these capabilities extended to protein annotation. We assigned different frontier generalist models a variety of protein annotation tasks, including predicting the presence and coordinates of Pfam domains, loss of functional catalytic residues, and predicting structure and activity. On all annotation tasks, the frontier models performed well above chance; we did not benchmark them against specialised tools. The models also make characteristic hallucination errors, and they state them as confidently as their correct calls. Though untested against specialised methods, the nascent ability of frontier models to perform protein annotation from sequence alone is intriguing. The ability to reason over sequence, structure, and symbols in a single model allows for a neurosymbolic approach where a combination of sequence, experimental data and knowledge from the literature can be holistically combined to improve on de novo functional annotation of the protein universe. Prompts, test sets, model outputs and code: https://github.com/ai4curation/fable-sequence-to-function. Summary of results: https://ai4curation.io/fable-sequence-to-function/

candidates.title: Information Access and Gain-Loss Framing in Six Large Language Models and Human Decision Makers
candidates.abstract: A risky choice can be described by what will be saved or what will be lost, and people often choose differently depending on that wording. We test whether six large language models (LLMs) show this gain-loss framing effect, and whether it shrinks when they can first read more about the options. GPT-4.1, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Qwen3 235B and Llama 4 Maverick made 11,519 choices across four risk scenarios, each in its original wording, two paraphrases and a mirrored version in the opposite wording. Before choosing, a model could open up to 0, 2, 3 or 4 of seven information cards. With no cards, all six models showed large framing effects: the share choosing the safe option was 27 to 79 percentage points lower under loss than under gain wording. The gap was smaller at 2 cards than with no cards in every model. Against a 10-point threshold set in our analysis plan, GPT-4.1 fell within it at 4 cards and Qwen3 only at 2 cards; in the plan's pooled comparison over all versions, GPT-4.1 was within it from 2 cards and GPT-4o from 3. GPT-4o-mini and Llama 4 Maverick kept gaps of 28 to 66 points with cards, and for GPT-4o-mini and Qwen3 the gap grew again from 2 to 4 cards. Part of the drop from 0 to 2 cards may reflect a change in prompt format, and most card content counted against the risky option, which may favor the safe choice. In an exploratory comparison with 198 students who saw the same scenarios and cards but opened cards one at a time and chose how many, decisions made after opening 0 or 1 cards showed a 19-point difference between the gain scenarios, asked first, and the loss scenarios, asked later, and no clear difference appeared in decisions made after opening more, though this design cannot show that cards reduced framing in people. With these cards, in the balanced comparison 17 of 18 card gaps were below the model's no-card gap, but few were within the threshold.
candidates.comment: 19 pages, 3 figures. Code and model outputs: https://github.com/aadycm/Humans-Vs-LLM-Research

candidates.title: DisSparse: Pipelined Top-$p$ Sparse Attention for Long-Context LLM Serving
candidates.abstract: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by the memory demands of the key-value (KV) cache, whose size scales linearly with context length. Dynamic sparse attention reduces this bottleneck by fetching and attending only to a critical subset of tokens. The dominant primitive in dynamic sparse attention research and deployment is fixed-budget top-$k$ selection, which is favored because its deterministic block count aligns with the static memory allocation that systems like vLLM rely on. Top-$k$ uses a fixed budget regardless of how attention mass is distributed across heads, layers, and decode steps, leading to either wasted bandwidth on heads with peaky attention or dropped context on heads with diffuse attention. Top-$p$ (nucleus) selection adapts naturally to this variation but has seen limited adoption in production serving systems due to two system-level challenges: variable block counts that break deterministic block allocation and computationally expensive selection kernels that exceed the cost of attention itself. We present DisSparse, a serving system that integrates top-$p$ sparse attention into vLLM end-to-end. DisSparse decouples block selection from the scheduler's critical path, hides selection latency behind layer computation via a two-stream pipeline, and introduces a single-pass histogram-based top-$p$ kernel. We further observe intra-block sparsity, the inflation of selection budgets caused by mixing high- and low-importance tokens within fixed-size KV cache blocks, and address it with a token relocation kernel guided by accumulated prefill attention scores. Across long- and medium-context benchmarks on multiple models, DisSparse achieves 1.17x to 1.80x speedup in sparsity analysis (block selection) over state-of-the-art top-$p$ methods with negligible accuracy loss and supports up to 8x larger maximum batch sizes than dense vLLM under the same memory budget.

candidates.title: Environment-Aware Probabilistic State Estimation of Continuum Robots from Planar Imaging
candidates.abstract: Continuum robots are compliant along their entire length, making them well suited to navigating confined environments where contact with surrounding structures is often unavoidable. However, this compliance makes their modeling more complex compared to rigid robots, especially under contact, so their state must often be estimated from information available during operation.
